utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before we begin today, there is a matter which I want to deal with now, because it is becoming urgent. I understand that Witness C-036, it's proposed, should be the witness after next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that the next witness is comparatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is also correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have had the opportunity to consider the application under Rule 92 bis, and the conclusion that we've come to is that this is not strictly a matter of record or background, that the evidence which the witness gives deals with some matters which are very much part of the story in this case, and therefore it is better that all matters be dealt with live. Now, we recognise too that there is a great deal of evidence which this witness can give, and therefore there is a difficulty for all parties in dealing with the amount. We would wish the Prosecution to look again at some of their exhibits. As the amicus has pointed out, the relevance of some of them is doubtful. It's difficult -- or it's, rather, easier for the Prosecution to gauge the importance of these various documents than it is for the Trial Chamber. But a question we would ask is whether it really is necessary to produce this number, volume, of orders of the SAO Krajina. Provided the documents -- some documents are produced to show that it was operating as an entity, then it really must be a question of doubtful relevance whether it assists to have many more documents making the same point. So we would be grateful if the Prosecution would consider that. And we have to say that we are concerned about the length of time which this witness may take, and therefore, we will have in mind the operation of some sort of time limit. We don't wish to do that, but we've got to look at the overall length of this case and the amount of time which this witness may take which may be removed thereafter from some other important witnesses. So with all those matters in mind - I don't believe you're dealing with this witness, but perhaps you would pass that on to whoever is - and we will return in due course to any matters which require decision when the witness is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will pass on the Chamber's concerns and we will adapt the presentation of the evidence accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to reinforce what the Presiding Judge has said, I want to refer to a term used by Mr. Nice, "a library of documents." In my view, that's not the purpose of a trial, to establish a library of documents. We want evidence that is strictly relevant for the purpose, and we are concerned that in seeking to establish this library, we may be letting in evidence and documents that are not strictly essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like once again to bring up the question of looking at the order of witnesses. Apart from the one you mentioned just now, I haven't got any of the witnesses that you have announced, and I have no idea who the forthcoming witnesses will be. I just know about today's, which is 034, and I know about C-036, because I've been receiving documents for him - I received some the day before yesterday and in the course of these days - large piles of documents. As to the other witnesses, I haven't got any information at all as to when they're going to be called, and as far as I was able to understand, on several occasions you concluded that I should at least be given material for seven or eight witnesses in advance, for a week in advance. And once again, that has not been the case in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I understand the position to be this: That 036 is going to take at least a week, so that matter is covered. But it's obviously right that you should have notice. Mr. Groome, can you let the accused and the Trial Chamber have notice of the witnesses to be called after 036, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll provide that information after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Lazarevic, sorry to keep you waiting while we deal with those matters. Mr. Milosevic, you've got, I understand, an hour and three quarters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, yesterday, finally, at my insistence, you managed to identify at least some people in that group, the group that you call the anti-terrorist detachment, or as you refer to it as the group, the dirty jobs. And you said Sinisa Martic was one of them, and his nickname was Paraga. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Lazarevic, my information tells me that Commander Sinisa Martic does exist, that's true, but that his nickname was not Paraga, but Silt. And that that particular commander, Sinisa Martic, was never in the 21st Corps at all. Now, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Silt was the commander of the anti-terrorist unit on Banija, not in Kordun. Mr. Paraga, who in 1995 was killed in Topusko, was the commander of the anti-terrorist group in the 21st Corps. And I attended his funeral. If I remember correctly, the name of the person buried was Sinisa Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that you have picked up some rumours here, but Sinisa Martic was not the Paraga that you were talking about. There is no doubt on that score on the basis of the information and facts that people who are acquainted with the matter have been putting forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness has just said that's not right. He's told you what the answer is. Now, if you've got some other evidence, you can call it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to hear your comments on this matter: Yesterday you spoke about the armaments, the rifles, to Mile Bosnic, et cetera. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have received a written denial from Mile Bosnic, and I would like to hear your comments to that. I'm going to hand it over to you straight away. He signed it. And I should just like you to hear its contents. What he says is: "Mile Bosnic, former member of the Main Board of the SDS Krajina, president of the municipality of Slunj, deputy minister in the government of Borislav Mikelic. "Denial: I know Mr. Lazarevic from Velika Kladusa, but not as an officer of KOS but as an interpreter in the Agrokomerc company of Velika Kladusa and an interpreter in the Kordun Corps. It is strange that he was an officer of KOS when, from the age 18 up until 1984, he was an emigre. Lazarevic had --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. What does that comment mean? What are you putting to the witness; that he wasn't an officer of KOS?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, you weren't here yesterday. Of course he didn't work for it, because nobody in KOS knows about anybody by the name of Slobodan Lazarevic. And he's working for somebody else, that's quite obvious, but we'll get to that in due course. I should like to read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you deal with that, for me, at least? Just explain the position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I have been working. The denial that Mr. Milosevic just read to the Court specifically says that I have been emigre from the age of 18. However, in possession of the Prosecution are my military booklets, which states very clearly that at 18 I was serving my compulsory military service in the town of Kraljevo, from 1966 to 1968, which makes me 20. This gentleman states that at 18 I left the country already. So this is absolute ridiculous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the letter goes on to say as follows: "Lazarevic had nothing to do with me with respect to weapons by the JNA and the police force because I didn't have any contacts with him whatsoever, nor did I ever, even from Lazarevic, able to receive military weaponry. That is a lie. No rifles, no bombs, no Skorpions, no Motorolas. Never did I get any of this equipment from the man. And no group in Velika Kladusa was ever established or armed. And by that score I was not able to take part in arming anybody or to receive weapons from anybody or to plan any operations of any kind. I left Velika Kladusa of my own free will and in my apartment no weapons were found, nor did I have any problems in Kladusa or need to arm myself and execute operations. "Mr. Lazarevic probably knows that up until the second half of November 1991, I was not in contact with any JNA officer because I considered that their stand was neutral and that they were not helping us at all. He also knows that for these same reasons I was not on good terms, or rather, I was in a conflict with the gentleman from MUP, because they communicated --" and it says in brackets Milos and Toso Pajic -- "they communicated with the MUP of Croatia, so I wasn't able to obtain weapons from them either directly or via somebody else. "In October and November 1991, I was the director of Radio Television Petrova Gora, and therefore I had nothing to do with weapons there either, or the arming of Velika Kladusa or anywhere else. From the liberation of Slunj onwards --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is supposed to be cross-examination, not the reading out of statements. You can put what's in the statement, of course, to the witness, but he must have a chance to answer. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, dealing with what's been put so far, you see what's put; that this man had nothing to do with arms, no weapons were found in his apartment. Perhaps you could deal with that, first of all, if you've got any comment, and then go on to deal with what's in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The letter also states that Mr. Bosnic had no connections with me whatsoever. Again, it's a blatant lie, because Mr. Bosnic and myself were co-organisers of a cultural society in Topusko in early 1991 called Savo Mrkalj. I had a membership card with the number 9 on it, and organising committee had ten members, which clearly points that Mr. Bosnic and myself have been frequently together. The fact of the matter is Mr. Bosnic has received weaponry, and his claim there was nothing found in his apartment when he left Velika Kladusa can only mean that he took it out with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to say about any other matter? That he was in conflict, he said, with the MUP, so he couldn't obtain weapons from them. He was the director of the television and had nothing to do with weapons there either. Is there anything you want to say about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very simply, he had a very good cooperation with the MUP, directly with Mr. Toso Pajic. Why is Mr. Bosnic denying, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He goes on to state, Mr. Lazarevic: "From the liberation of Slunj, on the 19th of November, 1991 --" that means after the military operation -- "I became president of Slunj, the mayor of Slunj, and I had nothing to do with weapons once again. The events in June 1992 occurred in Jelov Klanac, where the Ustasha terrorist group killed five civilians. Amongst them was a little girl, age 14. The burial took place with a police and army guard present. "Between Cetingrad and Sturlic, a crime took place in November 1991, when 11 persons were killed, all of them from the Slunj locality. In May 1992, 15 people were killed from the Slunj area around Cetingrad. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Having seen Lazarevic in The Hague and hearing his lies about myself and others, and the people I belonged to, the question looms again that I would like to ask Lazarevic: Did he flee from Kladusa because of his gambling debts or because he was persecuted as a Serb? I know why he fled, and this brings me to another question I would like to ask him: Did he sell out his religion for a good meal --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all -- just a moment, Mr. Lazarevic. Let's just go through it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first point that's made is that this man was the president of Slunj, he said, where he had nothing to do with weapons, and then he makes some allegations about what happened there. Is there anything you want to say, first of all, about Slunj or this man's involvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. There's nothing I wish to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Then we move on, yes, to matters again he put about Slunj. Then he says that you have been telling lies about him. We've dealt with that. Then he comes to a question. What this man seems to allege is that you left Kladusa for -- because of gambling debts, seems to be the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I have to say, Your Honour: Mr. Milosevic is coming up with some absurd statement about my gambling debts which are absolutely incorrect. The day I have left Velika Kladusa was for the reason that I was in fear for my life, because I was daily observed and followed by the two brothers Brajdic, a well-known Croatian emigre from Sweden. I have contacted Vojnic over Motorola, picked up only with me, one of the guns which was given to me with a silencer on it, that was a Skorpion, and walked from my place of living to the border with RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you have any gambling debts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not, sir. Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose the next question is: Do you in fact gamble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have been known to sit down with friends and have a couple of games of poker. There's nothing unusual about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not to the extent -- but not to the extent which I would have to leave the country or the area because of the gambling debts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we continue, Mr. Milosevic is reading from a letter, and I'm quoting from a portion of it. This is Mr. Bosnic saying, "Questions I would like to ask Mr. Lazarevic," and it seems that he's going through a series of questions. I would submit that it's not for Mr. Bosnic to mail in his questions. It's for Mr. Milosevic to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty is we're dealing with a litigant in person, and whereas that might be right for an advocate, we have to adapt the cross-examination to allow for that. We take it, when these matters are read out, that these are questions which the witness himself -- or the accused, rather, himself is putting, and we allow him to do it in that way. An advocate would be allowed to put a statement, but of course he would have to do it in interrogatory form. This accused clearly can't do that, finds it difficult. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What else have you got from that statement, please, that you want to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's another question in it, and it says the following: For a little bit of money and a new identity, has he agreed to be a liar at that so-called court? And what sum is he lying for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need this man's comments about the Tribunal, thank you. It may be this has been put before, and since I was ill yesterday, I didn't hear it, but you should be able to deal with it. It's suggested that you've, for money, really, that you've told untruths, Mr. Lazarevic. Very briefly, perhaps you could deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour, absolutely at any given time or moment, I have been offered by the Prosecution immunity, money, or any other benefits from my testifying. I have done this absolutely voluntarily because I believed that the man who is responsible for untold tragedies in the area of Balkans should eventually reply to the accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we have heard here from the opposite side that you have been given a new identity and a new country of residence, and so on and so forth. So it's not my assertion; it's what that opposite side over there stated. And I assume you know that, you're aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Again you're not correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we all had occasion to hear what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. May, here is the letter. I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've ruled on these matters before. If you want to call Mr. Bosnic, you can. We're not going to exhibit letters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. This doesn't present any difficulty to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have another denial here, and I would like to read that out too. It is a denial sent in by Borislav Mikelic, the former Prime Minister of the government of Srpska Krajina and now president of the Committee for Displaced Persons, a non-governmental organisation. That's what it says in the heading of this letter: "Since, as the Prime Minister of the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina with two other ministers in the government --" and in brackets it says the Minister for the Interior and the Minister for Defence -- "in the period from the 20th of April, 1994 until the 29th of May, 1995, was a member of the Supreme Council for Defence of the RSK, and that body was also made up by General Milan Celeketic, as commander of the General Staff, Milan Martic as the president of Republic of Srpska Krajina and also president of the Supreme Defence Council of the RSK, I consider it to be my duty to deny what Mr. Lazarevic said before The Hague Tribunal on the 30th of October, 2002. The first is that the Serbian army of Krajina was under the direct command of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia and General Momcilo Perisic, and the second is that the people from Kordun and part of the 21st Corps of the Serbian army of Krajina was unable to find themselves in an encirclement to leave that area via Croatian territory in going to the SR of Yugoslavia [as interpreted]. Point 1 response to the assertion that throughout that period of one year -- I say with full responsibility that throughout that period of one year, which is the time I was Prime Minister of the government and member of the Supreme Defence Council, at meetings of the Supreme Council of the army of SRK we did not receive a single order nor did we receive a single order or instruction from the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia or from General Momcilo Perisic either. So I say with full responsibility will the army -- that the army of RSK was commanded by Milan Celeketic and he had six corps of the Serbian army of Krajina under his command," and he goes on to enumerate all these units. I want to save time and not enumerate all the units, but I should like to stress that the head of the General Staff was General Dusan Loncar, and the Defence Minister Dr. Rade Tanjiga. "All military decisions that were taken at that time related to the defence of the RSK and questions of the material position of the Serbian army were subject of discussion at the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. If some of these questions stepped out of these frameworks, it was the arbitrariness of individual people who were in command positions in the army of the RSK and the General Staff of the JNA had nothing to do with it. I should also like to say in my denial that Mr. Lazarevic, according to my knowledge, was just an interpreter for the Kordun area in the relationship between the civilian and military authorities in the RSK on the one side and on the other side members of UNPROFOR and international humanitarian organisations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll pause there and we'll deal with those matters. Mr. Lazarevic, you should have the opportunity to answer this. This is a man called Mikelic who writes, or claims, apparently, that the army of the RSK was commanded by Cekic, had six corps under his command, there was no order from the General Staff or from Perisic, all military decisions were taken relating to the defence of the RSK at meetings of the Supreme Defence Council. That's the first point that's made. The second one, if you would wish to deal with it, is that if there were questions, it's put, out of the framework, it was due to the arbitrariness of individual people. So what is being put is that there was no question of control by -- or involvement by the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, that this was an independent body at the RSK, but some individuals may have acted outside this framework. That seems to be the point. Perhaps you would like to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be very brief about this. Undisputed fact that hundred per cent of high-ranking officers within the RSK army were active officers of JNA, which later became VJ, that they were on the payroll of the general headquarters in Belgrade, and it's also irrefutable evidence that Mr. -- Colonel Bulat, who was my CO, has been virtually daily on line with Belgrade, General HQ, and I have personally been present in his office when he spoke directly to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to spend any more time on this issue, since we dealt with it yesterday. My time is restricted here. And what this Prime Minister of the RSK wrote in fact confirms what I said yesterday, and in fact, it denies what you said. Point 2: Nobody disputed the fact that the officers of the RSK used to be the officers of the JNA, just as the Croatian officers used to be the officers of the JNA while the JNA still existed, and the same applies to the Muslim army. Muslim officers used to be officers of the JNA while the JNA still existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with this. We have the point that you made. The other point made is that they were on the payroll. This is what the witness says; they were on the payroll of the headquarters in Belgrade. But let's move on from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Economic aid has nothing to do with commanding, Mr. May, and you should know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely -- this man speaks of something else. I will skip this part that deals with the encirclement of Topusko. Namely, after, on the 4th of August, 1995, and not on the 5th of August, 1995, as Mr. Lazarevic claims, the Croatian military Operation Storm started. "Dramatic events led to the fact that 20.000 Serbs from Kordun found themselves in Topusko, together with some members of the 21st Corps of the army of RSK. In the meantime, on the 4th, 5th, and 6th of August, 1995, a large number of Serbs from Lika, Kordun, and Banija area, together with a largest part of military formations, left that area through the border crossing at Dvor on the Una River, and the fate of Serbs from Kordun, as well as some members of the 21st Corps, became quite dramatic, because Croat armed forces, on the 6th of August, 1995, destroyed the bridge on the Una River. Being unable to establish contact from Topusko with anybody else -" and I'll skip over this part; he goes on to mention UNPROFOR, Zagreb, and Belgrade here - "they established, through satellite telephone, contact with me, as the former Prime Minister of the government of RSK, the leadership of the MUP of Kordun, through Milos Pajic, via mobile telephone of Djuro Skaljac, and this connection went through Slovenia, established contact with me because they knew that I, as a former Prime Minister and the chief of the negotiating team with Croatia, had a satellite telephone which was loaned to me by Thorvald Stoltenberg. "After presenting the dramatic situation to me that applied to the fate of 20.000 Serbs and some members of the 21st Corps in Topusko, I very quickly established contact with the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, or rather, with Mr. Akashi, and asked for an urgent intervention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't deal with this. Do you know anything about what's being put here, Mr. Lazarevic? This is all what this man says happened; he was on the phone and this sort of thing. Do you know anything about this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of Mr. Skaljac establishing contacts with Milosevic. The contacts which have been established from the office of the UN headquarters in the sector commander of sector north, those I have been present to. In the office, apart from me, was Mr. Skaljac, Mr. Pajic, and Colonel Bulat. And I have very clearly explained who they talked to and what replies we've got. The only reason that we did get out, we should be eternally grateful to the UN forces, not to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, this is a denial written by Mr. Mikelic, not Milosevic. You probably confused the last names. What I just read out to you is something that was written by the former Prime Minister of the RSK government, whose name is Mikelic, not Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... last statement there that you have talked to Mr. Skaljac on the mobile phone and that you have helped with [indiscernible] and surrender of the 21st Corps, which is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What have I said? Tell me again, please, because I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat in Serbian, Mr. President -- former president. In this part of your presentation, you said that Mr. Skaljac established contact with you directly via mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With me? I am reading out to you the denial written by Mikulic, and when I say, "He established contact with me," I'm quoting, Mr. Lazarevic, what Mr. Mikelic said. I'm reading out his letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's absolutely pointless to have this argument. Now, let's move on to something else. No point arguing. We know exactly what's been said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like to take a look at this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it you want the witness to answer to? If there's something else in the letter you want him to answer to, you can put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the entire discussion that we had yesterday regarding what this witness said about 20.000 people being encircled and so on, this whole story is depicted in a different light in this letter, and I wanted to show this, because my claim is that this witness lied throughout his entire evidence and his statement, and this is just one example of it. We can continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment. No doubt in due course we'll have to make our mind up about that. Now, move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, were you ever involved in selling weapons on any occasion while you were there with the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you -- did you sell a pistol manufactured in Czech republic that used to belong to a man called Djuric and who by mistake ended up in the Serbian territory around Slunj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man claims differently. He claims that this is true, but you are denying this. All right. Now let us go back to another untruth, which is not difficult to establish, although this is true of every sentence that was uttered here. On page 19, paragraph 6, of your statement, you claim that Mladjo Karan, member of the DB who was sent to Krajina from Belgrade, commanded units of the military police. Please take a look at your statement, page 19. You say, in the last paragraph: "Mladjo Karan, member of the state security service, who had been sent to Krajina from Belgrade. KOS didn't like him very much, due to rivalry that existed between these two services." This is what you say on page 19 about Karan, who was not liked very much by the KOS, due to rivalry between these two services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 21 in English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you say in your statement, that KOS didn't like him due to the rivalry between these two services?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us go back to page 12, penultimate paragraph of your statement, where you claim -- and I'm again quoting what you're saying, so when I'm quoting something that somebody said, this is not something that I am in fact saying, this is just a quote. "In 1993 --" you speak here about Petar Surla, and the next sentence in that paragraph says: "In 1993 he was replaced by Mladjo Karan, who was in charge of KOS in sector north up until August of 1995." So here you say that he was from the DB, and this is why he wasn't well-liked by KOS, due to rivalry, and prior to that you said that he was the man who was in charge of KOS. So this is another untruth, Mr. Lazarevic, spread out by you. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are starting from an unbelievable position, which is that the whole world is lying and that you are the only one telling the truth. What I said is repeated throughout this statement of mine. I say that Mladjo Karan was a KOS colonel in charge of security in the 21st Corps. This is a small error that appeared here, where it says DB. It should have been KOS, not DB. And I presume that this error was beyond my ability to correct it. Somebody else was responsible for it. And this is the only instance where it says that he was a member of the DB. In all other instances, it says very clearly that he was a member of KOS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I need a copy of this. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's also a diagram which has been presented to the Court which very clearly states the position of Colonel Karan within the structure of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have it. 348 -- is it 348, tab 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we could quickly have that and refer to it. If it could go on the projector. Yes. Perhaps you would just point it out again, please, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see here, Your Honour, in the second square, saying Colonel Mladjo Karan, from 1993 to 1995, direct line leads to KOS command in Belgrade. He is nowhere on this graph connected to SDB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, and who drew up this diagram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are using your own diagram, the one that you fabricated and drafted, to prove something else that you have also fabricated. This is a diagram that was authored by you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comments to that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't either. All right, Mr. Lazarevic. Since you said that this was just a tiny error where it said "SDB," what I'm saying to you is that that's not the case. The error is not only that it says SDB, but in the entire sense of what you're saying, because you said here Mladjo Karan, member of the SDB, who had been sent to Krajina from Belgrade was not liked by KOS due to rivalry between these two services. So this is not a case of typo, an error whether it should be DB or KOS, but you are in fact speaking of a rivalry that existed between these two services and the reasons why Karan was not liked by KOS. So this is quite clear. Perhaps it's not clear to you, because this is not in fact your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm absolutely certain that this is the case of a very simple typing mistake. If you replace the SDB with KOS, then it would be absolutely clear what I have stated before, that there were two strains within KOS, one dealing with internal security, which was Mr. Karan, Colonel Karan, and the other strain by external security of the country. And this is where these two services within the same organisation had a little antagonism. So if this typing mistake is corrected to read "KOS," the statement is absolutely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I continue? Since this does not deserve any further explanation. On page 20, paragraph 2, you said that Ajdinovic fell out of favour at the end of 1994, early 1995, when he was arrested by the DB because he had taken an expensive reconnaissance equipment out of a drone that had crashed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Where was the drone, where did it crash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Glina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it crash?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who shot it down?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say -- the information that I have indicates that Ajdinovic not only was never arrested, he was even never detained, and that this high-priced surveillance equipment remained intact and could be sold because it was shot down by a rocket and fell from a great height. So how can you say something that is so entirely ridiculous? Is that what you're claiming, that despite this crash, this equipment remained intact? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me what is your question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently this drone must have been shot by some kind of artillery weapon. It must have been a missile, a rocket, or something of that nature. And after that, the drone crashed from great heights and the surveillance equipment remained undamaged and somebody has actually able to sell it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm claiming that in fact this drone was shot down, and this can be confirmed by UN documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what if it was shot down?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The talks that were led between the 21st Corps and other sides indicate that Colonel Ajdinovic was in fact arrested. I was never present there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how come do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Colonel Bulat and other officers told me about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every time I ask you how come you know of this, you reply that you had heard this from somebody. Now, let us turn to another very odd thing that you described. You talk about the exhuming of corpses in order to be exchanged with the Muslims. Is it true that for those purposes you exhumed 99 bodies and you -- you exhumed 90 bodies and you lacked ten bodies in order to carry out the exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that I exhumed all of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me from which location these 90 bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the territory of the entire RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the territory of the entire RSK? Now, tell me, please: Whose bodies were these? Were these bodies of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These bodies were those of members of the corps, 5th Corps, that were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please: How did Muslim bodies appear in the territory of RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the simple reason because the Muslim army was engaged in combat in the territory of RSK. The RSK army fought the Bosnian forces in that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are in fact referring to army of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that the army of RSK in fact took Muslim bodies to bury them in its territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that anybody went about burying these bodies. I'm just saying that they were delivered in order to be exchanged. It was quite normal for armies to do that, to collect these bodies of enemy's army in order to exchange them for their own bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I just asked you where were these bodies collected, and you said that that was on the territory of the RSK. The Muslims could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not have been killed in the territory of RSK, because they were never engaged in combat there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, these bodies were given to me on the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, these bodies were never in fact handed over to you, but we will get to that later. And now let me ask you this: Since you were in charge of the exchange, I presume that you have the names of people whose bodies, as you say, you exchanged.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't have those names, Mr. Milosevic. Most of these bodies were not identified at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't have the names. Now, please tell me: Since you claim that you were ten bodies short, and then Djuro Skaljac told you to go by the river near Vojnic and to exhume another four bodies there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuro Skaljac took me personally to the location where four bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near some small river. I can only tell you that it was about one to one and a half kilometres from Vojnic, in the direction of Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's also on the territory of RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have to remind you both to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will bear this in mind, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're saying that these people were killed by the policemen of Krajina. And who were these people whose bodies you dug out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I said in my statement were that four persons, four bodies, were dug out, that their arms were tied with a wire, and it was apparently a case of execution and not a case of somebody who got killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the identity of these people that you're referring to now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then on page 21, in paragraph 1, you say that you were given several bodies by Captain Sarac in Velika Kladusa, and you got to know this man through Arkan's colonel, Pejovic, nicknamed Peja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just find the bit that speaks of this. Colonel Pejovic, Peja, who sent you there, and then later on, on page 22, you mention him again, with a comment that he always treated you fairly, this man Pejovic, Peja. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's on page 22, paragraph 2, or perhaps paragraph 3, depending on how you count this. You say that he always treated you fairly, this man Pejovic, Peja, who helped you solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You forgot to mention one piece of information, which is that Colonel Karan sent me to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm now referring to this person Pejovic, who you say always treated you fairly. This is what I'm reading out of your statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Pejovic always treated me fairly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even describe him being blond, around 40 years of age, treated me correctly. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you said; right? Okay, then. Do you know what this Peja was called?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was called Peja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had another nickname. Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know it. I know him as Colonel Pejovic, known as Peja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel Pejovic, known as Peja. That is not disputable. That has been confirmed. Do you know that his comrades called him Peja Ciganin, or Peja the Gypsy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt very much that people from his team would call him Peja the Gypsy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they called him that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very relevant and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ask and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since you claim here, as you wrote: Blond, about 40 years of age, and so on and so forth. He was called that because he had jet-black hair and dark skin, and he was not blond at all, and you never saw him at all, and you just confirmed that that's the way you had described him, that he was in fact dark-skinned and dark-haired and that's why he had this nickname among his friends: Peja the Gypsy. So completely the opposite. Somebody sold you a story that you used here, whereas you never saw the man at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not following the question at all. What is the -- start again, Mr. Milosevic. And just to correct the transcript, 5 lines up, what I actually said was: Let him ask and we'll see, and that was in answer to a comment by the witness: Is this relevant? Fine, Mr. Milosevic, what are you putting to the witness? It's quite impossible to follow. And how is he going to assist us about this, decide this case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, he is describing Pejovic -- the witness is describing Pejovic, also known as Peja, as a fair-haired, blond person, whereas everyone who knew the man knows well that he had dark skin and jet-black hair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We get the point. We get the point. Colonel Pejovic, known as Peja. You have misdescribed him, it's said. Mr. Lazarevic, perhaps you can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the man who introduced himself to me, the first time that I met him as Colonel Pejovic, Peja, or called aka Peja, all of his officers, including Mr. Pejovic, had their hair cut very, very short. They carried a beret on their heads. My impression was that the man was blond. I would like to point out that I have been to Pauk on various occasions. I have met Colonel Pejovic at least three times, and always considered him to be a perfect gentleman. I have no idea why would anybody claim today that I have not met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the reason is obvious, Mr. Lazarevic. The reason is that your description is completely opposite to his real appearance. Is it true, Mr. Lazarevic, that other people you mention as having been in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, you only mention proving that by their presence on the public parade on the occasion of St. Vitus Day, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to explain your question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is very simple. I believe that you are speculating and misrepresenting facts. You have talked here about a number of people and shown photographs of people who, as you claim, were present on Petrova Gora, and the photographs show them on the parade in Slunj on the occasion of St. Vitus Day, which you also attended as an interpreter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did we establish that it was a public parade, broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just asked me a direct question whether I was an interpreter there. I said no; I was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Liaison officer, let it be.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let's not let it be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Lazarevic. Is it disputable that the parade was public?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it disputable that it was broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it disputable that it was on the occasion of St. Vitus Day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it disputable that guests were invited and that on the occasion of the holiday, guests are usually invited?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that, but not all of them were simply guests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it disputable that guests were there from Serbia, from Republika Srpska, from the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, namely, Bosnians from the army of Fikret Abdic, plus people from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and officers of the United Nations force, also from various countries? Is that disputable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not disputable either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So concerning Petrova Gora and who attended and all the things you did there, you produced evidence from a parade in Slunj which was public and attended by guests all the over the place; from Western Bosnia, from Serbian Krajina, from Republika Srpska, and from the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my statement regarding Colonel Pejovic refers to the command of Pauk in Bosnia. I never said for a moment that I met him at Petrova Gora. I said I met him in Pauk and that this command was partially represented at the parade. But let us go back for a moment to the exchange of those unfortunate hapless 100 people who had been killed in combat or executed, let's not go into those details now. The size of that exchange was such that it could not have been carried out without the participation of commands from both sides, the 5th Corps, namely, of the Bosnian army, and the 21st Corps of Kordun, and the 2nd Corps of Serbian Krajina, and a corps from Banija. It was equally impossible to carry it out without the presence of the United Nations representatives, who provided us with body bags. There are records, Mr. Milosevic, which will unequivocally prove --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I'm speaking from memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell me from memory. If you took over those bodies, I suppose they were Serbian bodies, the 99 bodies we talked about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we took over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that you took over from the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember or did you note down at least one Serbian family to whom you returned a family member of theirs, a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, all the corpses were automatically sent on to Bosnia for autopsy in Banja Luka, all the 99 bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know of a single name of a person who was exchanged then. Not a single one was identified or could have been identified. You don't know a single family that was anxious and interested to find out about these fallen fighters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the committee for exchange did not talk to families. They conducted discussions at level of commands and with the United Nations about how to ensure the fastest possible expedient exchange on a one-to-one basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that something like that never happened, that no one in the area which you refer to ever carried out such an exchange of corpses? I'm not saying that there were no exchanges of bodies during the war, but this exchange that you're talking about never happened in this area. Nobody knows about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parents of the people who were killed know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just made this up, Mr. Lazarevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you claim, then, that you were present at the headquarters in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that I was in the headquarters in Pauk, near Velika Kladusa, if that's the question you're asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not asking any particular questions. I'm just reading out your statement. You say: "I went three times to the complex in Petrova Gora," and so on and so forth. You mention Peja, saying that he was blond, whereas I say that he was black-haired. I'm saying that you -- I'm putting it to you that you never were in the complex at Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there. You forget that it was the headquarters of the 21st Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Corps before the arrival of the units from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know well, you claimed that a totally different place was the headquarters, and I refuted that, putting it to you that the command was in Petrova Gora, not in the place you mentioned. And now the tables have turned and you are claiming it was in Petrova Gora and I'm saying it was somewhere else. Shall we go on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we will not go on. I will explain to the Court why I am saying what I have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... of the 21st Corps, Your Honour. Originally, the 21st Corps was deployed. The command was placed at the top of the hill above the hotel in Topusko in vicinity of the UN compound. By the end of 1992, they have pulled out the command in Petrova Gora, military installation at the top of Petrova Gora. After the arrival of the special police from Serbia, this complex was given to them, and 21st Corps has moved again its command in vicinity of Vojnic. In one of the complexes that used to belong to Minister Spegelj, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I follow that. It may be important. Originally the command was in Topusko. Now, was there a stage where the command was at Petrova Gora, or did it go from Topusko to Vojnic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only command that apparently was prior to the formation of the 21st Corps would have been a command of the JNA forces, the 8th Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but, Mr. Lazarevic, I'm afraid I haven't followed this. You said originally the 21st Corps was deployed. This is according to the transcript. The command was placed at the top of the hill above the hotel in Topusko. So that's the first command headquarters. Now, after that, was the command moved to Vojnic? This is the 21st Corps. Have I understood that right, or was there an intermediary period when it was in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, between Vojnic and Topusko, 21st Corps was placed in the military installation in Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We discussed this yesterday. I don't want to waste any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Lazarevic, I explained to you yesterday, when you said that you were taken to the command of that Operative Group for the first time and explained that it was in a different location, I told you it was not correct either, because the command was in Petrova Gora, and we were talking about 1994 and 1995. Now, on page 24, you're talking about the kidnapping of French journalist, saying that you discovered that they had been taken by the special police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter hasn't caught the rest. Something is wrong with the microphones.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we try again? Can we try again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What shall we try again? What is it? What's the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try again. Ask your question again. Page 24, what was the question? The interpreters couldn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was talking about the spot where you refer to the kidnapping of journalists. Here is what it says. It's page 24 of your statement: "These two journalists were attempting to cross over from Bosnia-Herzegovina into the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The crossing was manned by special police from Serbia, namely, Stamatovic's men. Members of this special police arrested them when they attempted to cross over. These two journalists had permits from the Ministry of Information from the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Knin, allowing them to move around the Republic of Serbian Krajina. They stayed in sector north for a few days and then crossed over into B and H. Once they crossed over, they disappeared. Someone in Zagreb inquired about their whereabouts. Apparently the journalists had not contacted whomever they were supposed to contact, and so on. The Ministry of Information called me in Topusko, asking about the journalists' whereabouts. I knew that they had crossed over into Bosnia-Herzegovina but I didn't know what happened to them thereafter. We were suspected of having done something to them, which was not the case, so I started making inquiries in order to clear my name and the RSK involvement." And here comes the punch line: "I discovered that they had been picked up by the Serbian special police on charges of spying." I asked you a question a moment ago. You said you had discovered they had been picked up by the Serbian police on charges of spying and you are saying that it was not you who discovered it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Discovered," as you put it in your first question, seems to infer that I conducted my own investigation. The fact is that the commander in Topusko, the commander of UNPROFOR, had a very detailed description of these people. They described these people upon return to Zagreb, the people who had taken them. They gave a detailed description of the insignia, the sleeve patch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about the kidnapping of French journalists, you say that you discovered that they had been picked up by the Serbian special police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just now said that it was not you who discovered it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just explaining how it came about. You seem to be implying that everybody was counting on me to find out the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know who is counting on you, including today. I just quoted you a sentence which says: "I discovered that they had been picked up by the Serbian special police on charges of spying." That's what it says in your statement. So in conclusion, it is not difficult to conclude that you claim you discovered it because that's what you say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I discovered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's at least what you said yourself. What you say is correct, then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could the speakers be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked both to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in the next paragraph: "After they were released and got back to Zagreb, they sent their complaints, statements, to the RSK military police and UN HQ sector north. That is how I learned of their arrest." That's what it says. I have no doubt that it is precisely the way in which you found out about their arrest, but don't you see the inherent contradiction in the next sentence? You say that: "Based on their complaints filed upon their return to Zagreb, you learnt of their arrest. And in the sentence before that, you say that you had discovered they had been picked up by the Serbian special police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence in which this information is presented here is not necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Give a bit of a break to the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, they have enough interpreters, even when you're speaking Serbian. Their English is much better than yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have made very clear that the whole affair, when I was made -- when I have been informed about it, that is when I have started carrying some sort of investigation into what happened. The sector commander gave me a photocopy of the statements of the both French journalists, in which they have described, very clearly, the uniform and the shoulder flashes of the people that arrested them. Therefore, when I said that I discovered -- that I have discovered who committed this, it was based on a number of factors and evidence given to me. Now, it is quite possible that my statement here moved this way or that way, so it appears that one thing was said before, followed by something else. One sentence being placed on the top of the page or below the page by -- but I can repeat from word to word how this thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is not the first time that an error is made in drafting the statements. We've heard this a number of times yesterday and earlier today. But let us move on to the part of your testimony related to those international conferences. You said you are able to produce a diplomatic passport. Will you be so kind as to do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, a number of Mr. Lazarevic's passports were introduced as Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 7. I'd ask that that be shown to Mr. Lazarevic so that he may identify whether or not the diplomatic passport is among those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that what the accused was after was the originals. These are photocopies. Is that all you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just want to see the photocopy. I want to see this diplomatic passport. Where is the xerox copy? If you can just put it on the ELMO. I just want to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a several-page exhibit. I'd ask that the witness be able to look through the exhibit and preselect the page, if it's in there, that indicates it's a diplomatic passport.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Just let me see the front page or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness do that. You can ask your questions in due course, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have that, but it's not a diplomatic passport at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not telling the truth again. Where does it say here diplomatic passport?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer the question first before we go on. Yes. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, just indicate to us what that document is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is obvious from the document itself, it says "passeport de service" in French. [In English] [Previous translation continues]... travelling. My term being used as a diplomatic passport, actually, at the back of the passport, it does give me certain rights and privileges, not necessarily as an ambassador, nevertheless as an official passport of service of Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Your Honour, and clearly states that my place of birth was falsified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we got that when you were giving evidence earlier. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, a diplomatic passport and a service passport are two completely different things. He claimed he had a diplomatic passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's no good asking me or putting things to me. It's the witness you should be putting things to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, since you read out from the front page, the cover page, in French, "passeport de service," which means service passport, do you know that what it says on the diplomatic passport, actually, is "passeport diplomatique"; is that true, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably is, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know even that much?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never owned a diplomatic passport. I considered this a diplomatic passport of sorts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A diplomatic passport is so designated, and it is not issued only to ambassadors, but even the lowest ranking embassy and consular personnel, and even the clerk which puts visas into your passport with a stamp holds such a passport. Whereas the service passport is issued to technical auxiliary personnel travelling abroad on official business accompanying a delegation or something else, and even there, there is a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. big difference. The diplomatic passport is issued by the Foreign Ministry whereas the service passports are issued by the Ministry of the Interior, as any other passport. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is I held three passports I was issued with in Belgrade and which enabled me to travel abroad even later, after all those events, without ever being searched or stopped. In my book, it's a sort of diplomatic passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even that is not true, because even a diplomatic passport is no guarantee that you would not be stopped or searched if the customs officer has any doubt about you. The service passport was issued to you as part of the technical personnel, and that's what it says here, "Slobodan Lazarevic, interpreter." You got this passport because you accompanied a delegation to a conference in the capacity of interpreter, which leads me to believe that you are trying to deceive people here by saying that you have a diplomatic passport which seems to infer that you held a position which you never held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I said, that will be for us to consider, Mr. Milosevic. It says service personnel. He's described it as a diplomatic passport. If that's a point of any significance, we'll consider it. Now, it's time for the break. Half an hour. And you've got about 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, this false introduction is always a relevant matter if a witness presents himself otherwise than what he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour. Half an hour, please. Mr. Lazarevic, would you be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, just tell me, please, how much more time I have, according to your calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got, I think, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty minutes is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you've had quite a time to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but even in the most rigid interpretation of time, as we started out with this witness at a quarter to 10.00 and not half past 9.00, that would mean at least half an hour, because I had one hour and 40 minutes prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will look at that, but let's get on with the examination now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were describing, when it came to the international meetings that you had, encounters, how the consultations took place with the official representatives of Yugoslavia and Serbia. You described how you would go to a hotel, you stayed in a hotel, and then the military part of the group would go to the General Staff, the civilians would go to the government or, as you said it, at my cabinet or whatever, but go to the civilian authorities anyway. I think that was your description more or less; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally weren't present when these negotiations were taking place. All you knew was that a part of these delegations would go to the civilian authorities and others would go to the military ones to consult them about the forthcoming international conference.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would inform us where they had been for their briefings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew what they told you, otherwise you didn't take part yourself in these briefings; right? The briefings weren't held in your presence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. As we've cleared that point up, or rather, that claim that you made, let us take a look at what it says on page 14, in the penultimate paragraph. The last one is just one sentence, and the penultimate states as follows, and I'm going to read out what you say in your statement: "At those briefings -- at the briefings, I would read out the points on the agenda one by one. Then the representative of the Belgrade government who was present would give us our instructions. We were told if we could agree to a certain point or not, and if we could agree to something, then to what extent we were allowed to do so," and so on and so forth. So what you write here is in direct contradiction with what you were saying a moment ago, Mr. Lazarevic. Is that obvious to you or is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite obvious, and I have an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please go ahead and explain it to us, then.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the people who conducted the investigation that this be changed, because I never made a statement like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Once again you didn't make that statement, just like you didn't about the mine on the playing field of Topusko, so they wrote in something that you didn't say; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to err is human. People make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be quite clear. But let's move on. Let's move on. You also described, in detail, the meeting that you had on the 16th of June, in Geneva, as far as I was able to gather. Right? Is that correct, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described the fact that Goran Hadzic had called Zoran Lilic, president of the FRY, to consult him in that office that was full, all of you were present. And then somebody from the army, I assume, would call up somebody in the General Staff to ask them something. I think that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That referred to the meeting in Norway, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Only in Norway, then. And what refers to the meeting -- because the other side also took note of the fact that you described in detail the meeting on the 16th of June in Geneva. What refers to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to the meeting in Geneva, yes, and I was answering questions to the best of my recollections. Perhaps I made a mistake and Mr. Goran Hadzic was not at that first meeting, but there were minutes and they stipulate who was present. But as for Goran Hadzic, I can say with certainty that he was there, because I have a photograph with him and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; from Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about Norway now. I'm talking about Geneva. So what were you saying about Geneva?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the meeting was held, that it was a very short meeting; it lasted two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that no agreement was reached; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, looking at my notes and the information that I have, that I have received, the head of the delegation at that meeting in Geneva was called Novakovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military delegation? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that Hadzic attended the meeting?
