utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely sure, and I've said that quite clearly already. I answered questions according to the best of my recollections. Mr. Kosta Novakovic, Colonel Kosta Novakovic was the head of the military delegation, Mr. Milosevic, because there was a civilian delegation as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was a mixed delegation, in fact. As far as the civilians are concerned, according to my notes here, there was Bijacin [phoen], Srba Jarcevic and Paspalj. They attended that meeting, and the head was Novakovic. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as my information here tells me, that meeting was held under the auspices of General Belker [phoen], who was the commander of UNPROFOR at that particular time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct, then, that they decided to make a demarcation line, a separation line?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was a topic that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is not correct, that they had reached no agreement and that they were told not to reach any agreement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that seven days later we had another meeting, because nothing was implemented on the ground. So I would say that no agreement had actually been reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the basis of these notes here, Mr. Lazarevic, it says that you did not attend that meeting in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you are not right there, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I personally wasn't there, so I can't say, but that's what it says here. And you claim you did attend the meeting on the 16th of June in Geneva; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You in fact attended another meeting from the 6th to the 8th of July, did you not? Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were at that meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present at that particular meeting, then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The delegation increased in numbers after each -- at each subsequent meeting. I personally did not have list of all the people who were to be there, nor was I interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well according to this note that I received, it was the same delegation but it was a military delegation, not a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the delegations were always composed of the political part of the delegation and the military part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say that the notes I have here are not correct, that it was a mixed delegation on that occasion as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the topic discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some unknown reason, I keep remembering those unfortunate turbines around Knin, so it is quite possible that the discussion on that particular occasion were the turbines in Knin that had been sent for repairs to the Rade Koncar factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have here that it was a ceasefire that was discussed and a demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that means that at that first meeting nothing was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this was an ongoing issue and was always discussed. Now, tell me, please: Was Hadzic present at that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't attend the first meeting either.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. Mr. Milosevic, we're talking about some things that took place ten or eleven years ago, and I didn't keep notes and records about all those events. The fact is that I did attend the meetings, to the best of my recollections, and I can testify in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to note that what you just said does not coincide with the facts that I have by way of information. Now, whether that was so or whether that was not so -- what meeting did Galbraith attend? Because I don't have any information as to Galbraith's attendance anywhere.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was a mistake, or maybe in the transcript the interpretation might have been wrong. So I'd like to remind you what you say on page 14 about the event when you speak about Hadzic. As you explained here, Galbraith began by saying, "Mr. President," and then he said that there was a dispatcher of some kind, words to that effect. You said this out live in the courtroom. I haven't got the transcript in front of me, but I assume you remember what you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. He did say that, because it was a very important statement that he made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. However, as you know, he was not a dispatcher of any kind; he was in charge of a warehouse, a warehouse clerk, and that was his post, his job, that he was a warehouse clerk. Do you know that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't say he was a dispatcher of any kind, and in any literary or figurative sense, but what he was doing was stating the job he did and his calling. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't understood as such in the context, because when they addressed him as "Mr. President," he said, "I am not a president, I am a dispatcher."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that that's what Galbraith asked him about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambassadors, the US ambassadors, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's see what it says in your statement. "The international conferences that I attended were during the period when Goran Hadzic was president of the RSK. Hadzic had been a warehouse --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word in Serbian that the accused is using is "magazinar," which has been translated as "dispatcher," interpreter's note. That's on page 14 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist the Court. The English version is on page 15, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, and I'm reading what you say. "Hadzic was a warehouse clerk, and he was --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or dispatcher, as it says in the statement, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- before the war and was really a very raw peasant. He was more interested in chasing women, in getting drunk and in making money than in administering a government. He knew he was in over his head, and on one occasion when I addressed him --" "I" is you. "On one occasion when I addressed him as 'Mr. President,' he replied, 'I'm not a president, I'm a dispatcher.'"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "magazinar" is the word in Serbian that the accused is using, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore you are claiming something quite different here. He was not addressed by the Canadian or whatever other ambassador - you mentioned a few of them a moment ago - and Galbraith wasn't at that meeting at all. But you yourself, you say that you addressed him and that he responded and said he was a warehouse clerk, which in fact he was before the war, because that was his job. That was his profession. Isn't that right, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says literally, "On one occasion," and that occasion is the occasion in Norway, Mr. Milosevic. So I said, "On one occasion when I addressed him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you say, "On one occasion when I addressed him." So you addressed him and it was no ambassador who addressed him. And he said -- you addressed him as "President" and his reply was, "I'm not a president; I'm a warehouse clerk." Now, why do you say that it was an official contact between him and some ambassador when it says quite plainly here it was a conversation between the two of you in a delegation in which you were an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have been quite clear in giving my statement, and I have repeated it several times, because it was a very specific one. I said that that occurred in Norway, that Mr. Hadzic was sitting down at the table and playing solitaire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether he was playing solitaire.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking when it happened, what I'm asking is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic is interrupting the witness and not permitting him to finish his answer. I'd ask that he be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness finish the answer. Anything you want to add, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only one thing, Your Honour: It did happen in Norway. I have never met Mr. Hadzic in a man-to-man kind of unofficial situation to discuss anything with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lazarevic. I'm not claiming that you met him in any unofficial capacity or occasions. I'm just reading from your statement, and it says quite literally, word for word, that when you addressed him, he told you that he was a warehouse clerk, which in fact he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you said that Galbraith addressed him and then the Canadian ambassador and then some other ambassador, that that was his response, you were in fact telling an untruth; isn't that right, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. That is completely untrue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, is this how you put it in your statement if what you said here, the oral testimony, is the absolute truth and it is in contradiction with what it says in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see no contradiction. It says on one occasion or in one instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That instance or occasion. But you're talking about the ambassador and not about yourself. So I assume there's a difference as to whether he talked to the ambassador of a foreign country or with you who were working as an interpreter for him at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't talk to the ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that he did.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambassadors addressed him through me, and Mr. Hadzic's reply was to me, he didn't even look at the ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Fine. But you said that you addressed him, and not the ambassadors. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time. This is a trial which is going to last a very long time. It will last even longer with you taking points of this kind over and over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that in Norway, and I have a list here, that Hadzic, Jarcevic, Kuzet, Rakic, Novakovic, Vujinovic, Ergic, all those people, the military and civilian delegation, and then from Croatia, Sarinic, Ucekovic, the officers Domazet and Stipetic, and the mediators were Vollebaek, who replaced Stoltenberg, Ahrens, who was a replacement for Lord Owen, Bo Pellnas, and Jeannie Peterson. There you have it, there you are, that's what it says. So I can't see any trace of this man Savo Milosevic whom you seem to have included. And could you explain who this man Savo Milosevic is? I do know one Savo Milosevic. He is the football player on the national team who gives very good goals. I know him from television, but I don't know which Savo Milosevic you're thinking about. I assume that this Savo Milosevic of ours that gives such good goals was not the one in question. So who is your particular Savo Milosevic? I haven't got him in this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have a very good sense of humour. Whether it was Savo or Miso, what his first name was, I don't know, but this man was introduced as the host at both the meetings in Geneva. And you must allow for the possibility that at the meeting in Norway there was a group of observers who had no official capacity within that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you have attributed the presence -- some importance to that presence, so not an observer status or even - how shall I put this? - the role of a host, I think you said, but you ascribe something else to the presence. And then you said they mention me, and this man Savo Milosevic mentioned me, and he referred to me with the name Slobo. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just him. Out of all the other members of the delegation, this was just him, him and several other million Serbs who also call me Slobo, which I hope you know. I hope you're aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually it was in a very negative context when they called you Slobo. I'm surprised that you brought that up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that's your opinion, but I don't think that's what those people think. And do you know that nobody referred to me as "boss" or "chef," nobody from my entourage, especially nobody from the Republika Srpska or RSK either. Absolutely nobody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most people in the RSK who were down there referred to you as "boss," or "chef." That was your official nickname in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lazarevic. I'm sure you know that far better than I do, so let's not go into that any more. Tell me this: As you claim that they were instructed, they had received instructions not to accept any proposal, any agreement -- is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why, then, did they invite anybody, or allegedly call up people to consult them, if they had instructions that they had received beforehand not to accept any proposal? Why, then, would they call up and hold consultations? All they were supposed to do then was to obstruct, as you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called up for one reason, because usually they found themselves in a situation where they had no response to some concrete specific questions. They didn't know what to say, how to respond, and that's why they called you up, your assistants, associates, Perisic, Stanisic, et cetera, all the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, who did they call up in my cabinet? Did you ever learn that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You had millions of associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there were millions of aides in my cabinet? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Right. This is a very interesting point that you're making. And those people opposite say that I was working in an empty office, without any aides at all, and you claim that I had countless aides. That's a very good -- that's rich.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people who shared your offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume in my cabinet there are some sort of assistants and aides giving instruction, at least according to you. But let's not dwell on that. Tell me this: As you say that Belgrade insisted on being given an agenda beforehand, isn't it logical that when an international meeting is being held that an agenda is supplied beforehand and not people being invited and then being faced with an agenda? I assume that agendas are always regularly sent out prior to international meetings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical for the agendas to be received in advance, but it's not logical that third countries require an agenda and ask for an agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that anybody from Belgrade insisted upon having an agenda in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the officers, politicians that I encountered, because the boss has to decide what we do and don't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that you -- this is something you have conjured up yourself, Mr. Lazarevic. You've made it up. Because it's quite obviously not true. You couldn't have heard about that from anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what he said happened, Mr. Milosevic, so no point commenting on it. Now, we'll give you an extra five minutes, since you asked for it. You've got five minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that that is too short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on quickly, then. In 1995, after the Storm operation, you came to Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you began working for a company called the LCI in Belgrade, where the headquarters were in London, and the owner was Steve Dickson; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was in November and December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it also true that the main manager of the firm in Belgrade was Aleksandar Margetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that that particular company sent in to the municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. SUP, or the police in Belgrade, a criminal report, and that a warrant was issued in your name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And afterwards, is it true that you worked in the five-star firm in Ustanicka Street, with headquarters there, with Ivanka Golusin at the Hotel Serbia and this particular woman was in detention because you were involved in a scheme with sharing arrangements in Serbia. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With an apartment in Vojvodina, you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sold, in Vojvodina and Serbia, time-sharing schemes. In Serbia but especially in Vojvodina province; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. After this firm, did you register your own firm, which was called Melbourne, with its headquarters in the Novi Belgrad district?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also incorrect that these non-existent apartments in Malta and Spain, you took money from Darko Djuk to the tune of 30.000 Deutschmarks and other 65.000 Deutschmarks, et cetera. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If anybody knows anything about a time-share, there is no possibility that one person would spend $65.000 on one week in a share scheme of apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not go into that. I asked you about this. You said that's not correct. And we can continue. I don't mind you saying it's not correct, it's not true. Is it also not true that due to all of these reasons, there was a search warrant issued by the SUP of Belgrade for you due to the crimes that you committed? Was there a search warrant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. You said that the first warrant was issued in November of 1995. I lived in Belgrade until the year of 1999, in the same place, in the same address, and are you actually implying that no -- people from SUP were unable to find me for four years and I went to work every day in a regular fashion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lazarevic. We saw that there were a number of examples where you claim that there were errors in your statement and you don't know how they got into your statement. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I said was that when I quoted several examples in your statement, you told me that you didn't know about these things and you don't know how that got into your statement. That was the case with the mine on the soccer field in Topusko, and other examples. You claim that there were a number of things that got by accident into your statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several errors in my statement, and obviously one of them was a typing error where it said that Colonel Karan was a member of the DB instead of KOS. Yes, errors are there in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also said that nobody ever mined the soccer field in Topusko, for example.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I said that I never stated that. I said that about Glina. I don't know how that got into my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you actually saying that your -- the current arrangement is such that they don't even have to ask you what should be put in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of arrangements are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arrangement you have with the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no arrangements with any side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, there is something I cannot explain, and I will ask you to explain it for me. Your argument is that Serbs from 21st Corps killed other Serbs in order to fire up the situation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't believe that any Serb would state something like that, and that's why I want to ask you this: Do you know that people killing their own people was a tactic used during the war in Bosnia by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant, Mr. May, because I believe that this practice of killing their own people, which was typical for the Muslim side during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and similar false accusations that Serbs were guilty of that too; therefore, this practice and accusations of this nature indicate that all of this is coming from the same kitchen, is cooked in the same kitchen. It is all coming from the same source, those who incited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who are you suggesting has been involved in this conspiracy, this kitchen, as you put it? Who are you suggesting is responsible, so we can put it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, among others, the opposing side participated in that kitchen as well. This opposing side that formulates false indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let's turn to a specific issue. You had conversations with Curtis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your time is up. Your time is up, but we will allow that question, if it's about Mr. Curtis. You can ask it. But let the witness deal with this: What seems to be suggested is you've given your answer about Serbs killing Serbs due to a conspiracy which was going on to make allegations of that sort, involving the Prosecution. Could you just briefly answer as to whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is this question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you deal with it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Prosecution has nothing to do with any conspiracy against Milosevic. And me, as a witness, I'm trying just to contribute to actual truth being established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you can ask one more question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. If I'm allowed just one question, then, Mr. Lazarevic, tell me: Who are you working for today? Or let me make it more precise: How long have you been working for the British service for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very, very unusual question. Of course I don't work for British intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any questions from the amicus?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I will try and remain within the time limits that I was allotted, that I have been allotted so far. I will try to adhere to that. And my second point is that I would ask Mr. Lazarevic to always reply to me in B/C/S so that I would be able to control the flow better. Thank you. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lazarevic, as amicus curiae, I was unable to conduct an investigation of my own. I have no right to do that. And everything I would like to put to you has to do with things that were already brought up in examination-in-chief and those matters that are contained in your statement. This is what I will use as a basis for my questions. Therefore, I would first like to ask you to tell us this: This diagram that you drafted, was it drafted at the time when you gave your statement in January and July of 1999, or just now, when you had your interviews with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of it was done in January and February, and then all the way up to July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the diagram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am talking about the diagram. So part of it was done then and the other part was completed now, just seven or eight days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This set of exhibits that we dealt with over the past few days contains documents that have to do with 1993, 1994, and 1995. There is not a single document there pertaining to other periods of time. What I would like to know is whether you have any document that has to do with that diagram and that has to do with the time period from the 1st of August 1991 to June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to draw up such a diagram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any written evidence, primarily, or any other evidence, that could be used to establish that there was a plan for conducting ethnic cleansing and other crimes in August of 1991? Did you have any kind of evidence that would support this in your possession?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you worked for KOS - that's a service of the JNA - for exactly 30 years, from 1968 to 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, and you as well, to take a look at page 32, paragraph 3, of the English version of your statement. It's on page 29 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is as follows: During those 30 years, or shall we say two or three years less than that, when you received money for your activities, have you ever met people from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the country, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside of the country?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you ever met anybody from KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; Colonel Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said here is that: "In 1995 I went to Zimonja's office for the first time."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the first sentence in that paragraph. And the second one is -- the last one is: "Had something happened to him or had he disappeared, I would have known no one else to contact within KOS." Does that mean that during those 20 or 30 years, you had just a single contact person in KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zimonja, I would meet with him or with somebody pursuant to his recommendation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said here had he disappeared or had something happened to him, nobody else would know that you used to work for KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that nobody would know that I worked for KOS. It's just that I wouldn't know who else to contact in KOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 29, and in English it's on page 32, paragraph 2, it's just a paragraph before the one that we just dealt with. You said that you used to work -- that you worked for Zimonja until June of 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. All right. But then you said that until 1998, when I was finally issued with personal documents, IDs - that that was actually done in 1998.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in parenthesis, it says, "After I got these documents, I went to the US embassy for the first time." Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wanted to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the first time? Have you ever been there before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You turned over to the Prosecution a large number of photographs, and in your statement, at the end of your statement, it says that you turned over 90 photographs to the OTP. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most probably, yes. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in photograph 18, and I would like the Trial Chamber to take a look at the end of the statement of Mr. Lazarevic and to item 18. It says here: "A French captain --" you are describing the photograph -- "who spoke fluent Serbian. His parents were Serbs, but he was born in France. He served as the French battalion's liaison in the Bihac pocket. In this photograph, I am wearing a British uniform." Can you explain how come you came to wear the uniform of a British officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the time I collected uniforms, sir. I had a large number of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wore a British uniform when performing your assignments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an assignment. It was a private meeting in my apartment, and this is what's depicted in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. Could the Prosecution please allow us to take a look at that photograph when we get a chance. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, item 52, you say the man on the right side is Goran Gvozdenovic, who was in charge of 20 military police officers placed at my disposal. His father, Colonel Gvozdenovic was commander -- no, no. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. I skipped over. No. I'm sorry. Item 40. I apologise, Your Honours. It says here "Polish battalion and some Frenchmen." You're describing this picture. "Several Frenchmen, Danes, Canadians, during a Polish medal parade. I'm wearing a British uniform." How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also a function, and I believe that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you repeat the answer again. The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an informal function in Slunj, if that's the picture that I'm thinking of. I did wear a British uniform; however, I had the insignia of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We can verify that. But thank you anyway. And now I would like to go back to something that you mentioned yesterday concerning Bent Jenssen. That's page 25 of your B/C/S statement, and in English this can be found on page 27, paragraph 4. You said here in the beginning that you obtained from Bent Jenssen Croatian plans for the attack and he passed it to you the night before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you turn these plans over to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the staff of the 21st Corps; Colonel Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about something that cannot be found in your statement, which is that you were present when there was an attempt made to have talks with people, with Mr. Milosevic's cabinet, General Perisic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you were present on several occasions when a call was put through to the cabinets of Stanisic, Perisic, and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never once mentioned that in your 1999 statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in my 1999 statement there is a very detailed description of events that took place on the day of the withdrawal from Krajina. I very clearly said who -- what was the topic of those conversations and with whom there was a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, you said as follows: That you obtained those documents the day before, and then you go on to say that immediately after the attack started, a Croatian army major called Tihomir Tica, Brckan, called me, and then you describe what went on there. And the last two sentences go as follows: " Brckan told me to drive to Turanj with my wife claiming that he would ensure safe passage for us. He also told me to tell Bulat that the best thing to do would be to surrender. I explained that I couldn't cross over to the Croatian side due to the fact that my people would consider me a traitor, and then Brckan told me that he would send another liaison officer from Sisak and tell him about me so as to avoid any harm coming to me and my wife." So how is it that you had a conversation of this nature with the Croatian side the day after the attack started?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't take place on that day. It was very early after the attack started. Mr. Brckan called me on the telephone in the UN HQ and they came to inform me about this. Mr. Brckan was a liaison officer in Croatian army in the operational zone of Karlovac, and this is why we had very frequent contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who defined the direction in which the convoy of refugees started moving, 24.000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an agreement with Croatia that was reached between international organisations, north sector headquarters, ECMM, international organisations. Everybody was involved in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it a product of communication between you and your wife with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 27 in the B/C/S version; in the English version it's on page 30, third paragraph: "My wife proposed that we should reach an agreement with Croatians so that we can go in a convoy through Croatian territory, which is what we did." Did you in fact do this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and I explained the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were 24.000 people in the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deduced this based on various things; it doesn't have to be exact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that when you came to the border between Croatia and Serbia, you were the last one to cross over and that before you, between 14.000 and 15.000 people crossed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the convoy that you were in, that you escorted.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't escort it. I was in the fourth or fifth vehicle, at the head of the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But yesterday you said that you were the last one to cross.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was convinced that I was the last one to cross, because nobody came for an hour or two after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to those people that crossed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot explain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people only afterwards were put in a camp. They experienced some unpleasant things there. They were kept in the camp and tortured, as you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in another topic which is quite important. In your statement, you said, on page 1, that your first important assignment for KOS was the one in which you planted some films on a German citizen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that this was a German citizen vacationing on the island of Rab, and you simply came in and placed the rolls of film among his belongings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not interested in what happened to him afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many assignments of this nature you received?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't keep a record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But give us an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of similar tasks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, similar tasks that were given to you by KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't give you any figure concerning the assignments I performed over 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday we mentioned the brothers Brajdic on several occasions, and you said that you gave up on that task of killing them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on page 8 of the English version, paragraph 4, you say that you gave up on that assignment because of this: "The following day, after what happened in the bar --" and we talked about that yesterday -- "that same evening, the Brajdic brothers came by my house and parked their car across the street by the grocery store. They stayed there, watching my house from there." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you immediately had a desire -- or rather, you removed your wife from there and then you called Vojnic and then he told you to get away from there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened over the course of several days. It didn't all happen on one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't decide on your own to give up on this assignment. You simply realised that the Brajdic brothers were aware of what was about to happen, and in view of that, in view of the fact that there was a risk for you yourself, you put an end to this initiative.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you were in Agrokomerc for several years.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, six or seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And then only upon Abdic's return from prison you were fired, because a cleaning lady saw you taking out some documents from his office, and that's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your statement, on page 5, you said -- so page 5 of the English version, paragraph 2, you say that it was ironic that this was the reason for your being fired when in fact you had committed many other things, maybe not graver than that, but similar to that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was it was ironic that I was fired for something that I in fact did not do, when there were other things that I did do but was not fired for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And something that you spoke about the atmosphere of fear. I will just refer your attention to page 26, last -- so in the Serbian version, it's on page 26. You speak about how terror was sown here and that many things were fabricated. And then in one place you say that: "Rumour was spread out that Ustasha would kill all civilians, and I know about some individuals who in fact had a task to go around and spread rumours, such as that there are Ustashas going around slaughtering children." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that: "Under those circumstances, nobody will remain and try to -- see for themselves that that's not true. Simply, all of them will leave."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to say this: "I personally invented a story about civilians who had been massacred by Muslims from the 5th Corps in Topusko, which was broadcast by CNN as well." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I also requested that this part of this statement in the English version be removed. I said that there was an attack, and what I informed the CNN was that there was an attack on the 5th Corps which was moving in Kordun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why wasn't this paragraph removed from your statement? Why is it still here today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there is another matter that has to do with your contacts with ECMM in early 1992. I would just like to put this to you. Yesterday we touched on this, but we -- not all of us had your statement before us. And now I would like you to go to page 9 of the Serbian version, and page 10, paragraph 2, of the English one. His Honour Judge Robinson did not have the statement in front of him yesterday, and I would simply like to put to you what you stated here. You stated - and now this has to do with your contacts with the members of the ECMM. You said: "We did everything we could in order to establish a rapport with them, and then it made it much easier to have them accept our lies. No one would want to believe that their good friend would lie to them, so it made sense to use this approach, which I think we were much more effective with than were the Croats." Is that how you stated and is that how you worked?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go any further, we have got the two photographs to which Mr. Tapuskovic referred. Mr. Tapuskovic, just take a look at those photographs. Then we'll show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are those the photographs you had in mind, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other information than Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what is indicated on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness have a look at the photograph first of all. Now, we can have a look at that and we can see the extent of the uniform that was involved. Mr. Lazarevic, was that the uniform which you had? Don't show us for the moment. Just leave it there. Is that the uniform which you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- [In English] [Previous translation continues]... photograph. You can see that actually it's a combination of a number of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you can also see the JNA officers with me. Nobody really complained about me not having one of these uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Mr. Groome, is there any reason why those shouldn't be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It may be convenient. We can find a convenient way to exhibit them. It may be simply the next Prosecution Exhibit, since they're Prosecution photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or if the Chamber wishes, we can call them tab 15 and continue. The last exhibit that we used primarily with this witness is 348 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that. It's a good idea. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll mark it Prosecutor's Exhibit 348, tab 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And while we're on the subject of exhibits, I understand a statement hasn't yet been exhibited, hasn't been given a number, the witness's statement, and it should be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are actually two photographs now before, so should we designate those 15, 16, and the statement 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's do it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you -- would the Prosecution like the statement to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would ask that that particular statement be placed under seal, because it has some identifying information regarding the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will then be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 348, tab 17, under seal, confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One concern is that exhibits going under seal, of course, don't become public documents. We won't go into it now because we need to finish the witness's evidence, but perhaps you might like to consider how we deal with that in a more general way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion? Over the lunch break, may we redact the information that concerns us and then tender it as a public exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be a much better idea. Yes. Now, re-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you are a member of -- or work currently for the British intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have just one moment, please? May I ask the translator not to translate for me, please, because it gives me a double --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're free to remove the headset.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you are currently a member of British intelligence, and you said no. What I want to ask you is: Have you ever been a member of British intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any intelligence organisation other than KOS, the Yugoslav People's Army intelligence agency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, without giving us information so specific that it would identify where you are now, would you please briefly describe the nature of your employment at this time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I work as a security supervisor on one of the international airports outside of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic asserted that there were warrants for your arrest concerning some misdeeds that he alleges. I want to ask you to take a look at Exhibit 348, tab 7. That's your passport. And I want to direct you to one entry dated 1996 and three entries dated in 1997. If you would look and find those entries.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what those entries in your passport were for.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply a holiday. One was in Greece, and I believe the other one was in Malta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at any time -- excuse me. That passport is in the name of Slobodan Lazarevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at any time when you passed through the airport in Yugoslavia, were any warrants for your arrest ever brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic also read a list of names of people who were in -- who he claims were members of the delegation in Norway, and noted that a person by the name of Savo or Miso Milosevic was not included on that. I'm going to ask that Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 8, be placed on the overhead projector. And there are seven people depicted in this photograph. Of -- were all of the people depicted in this photograph members of the delegation that travelled from Belgrade to Norway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the seven people depicted in this photograph, how many of them were on the list read out by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means there are five people, at least on this photograph, that were part of the delegation but were not contained on the list read by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has suggested to you that when Mr. Hadzic referred to himself as a dispatcher, that he was referring to his employment, his actual employment, in a warehouse. My question to you is: At the time that Goran Hadzic made this statement to you, he was a sitting president; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any indication that, in addition to his presidential duties, he actually had continued his employment as a warehouse staff member?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask that you be shown a new exhibit, and perhaps it can be marked as tab 18. And there are copies for all the members -- or all the people who are in the courtroom here. I would ask that they be distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while that's being distributed, let me ask you a question. Mr. Milosevic presented a letter from a Mr. Bosnic, who claimed that in 1968 you were not in Yugoslavia, and you made reference to your military booklet. Can you describe for us what Prosecution 348, tab 15, is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a military booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose name is on that booklet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My own name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it indicate your years of service back in the 1960s?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, on the third page of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe those dates for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's a VP, meaning the military post 8977, the city is Kraljevo, and it goes from 29th of February, 1966, to the 12th of February, 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that just be placed briefly on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You referred to tab 15. It should be tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask that you be shown another document, and I'd ask that this be designated tab 19 and that copies be distributed to the Chamber. Mr. Lazarevic, I would ask you: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was signed by Colonel Cedomir Bulat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the substance of this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to prove for the benefits of a pension the number of years I have spent within the 21st Corps, which was the war zone, so I could get double time towards the pension funds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please read for us what it says regarding the period of time you served in the Kordun Corps, the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does confirm that me, Slobodan Lazarevic, had been in the war area as a member of the 21st KK, Kordun Corps, from 21st of December, 1991, to the 14th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Milosevic also asked you or presented you with a letter purporting to be from a Mr. Mikelic, and I want to ask you the following questions regarding that. You described a number of phone calls that were made on a satellite phone around the time of Operation Storm. Were you ever present when Mr. Mikelic was called?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, other than the satellite phone that Colonel Bulat used in your presence, was there any other satellite phone in the area of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That is the reason why we hired the office within the UN; so we can use the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that in Mr. Mikelic's comments to be placed before you, that he never did deny that General Perisic was in daily contact with General -- or Colonel Bulat? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in daily contact, yes. And if I may add that the last call which was made by Colonel Bulat to General Perisic was titled, "This is our last report from the field."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that indicate that it was unlikely that Colonel Bulat returned at some point later and then called Mr. Mikelic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time -- to whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were saying that the last call that Colonel Bulat made was actually --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last report. That's how he said, "This is the last report from the war," to the General Perisic. It explained the situation that we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any possibility that sometime after you left that office, that Colonel Bulat returned and had a conversation with Mr. Mikelic that you are unaware of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We all left the office together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the killing of Mayor Obradovic. Did you have occasion to see his body after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yesterday, put to you that police officers from the Republic of Serb Krajina were hired by the Republic of Serbia MUP almost as a favour or a way of assisting them during the course of the conflict. During your testimony, you described an incident where 400 to 500 RSK police officers were brought to Belgrade and used to put down a demonstration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not true that I asserted that the police of the Republic of Serbia hired out or rented out policemen to Serbian Krajina. It says here the policeman of Serbian Krajina were hired out from the police of the Republic of Serbia. I never said that yesterday, and it's not true. I invoked yesterday the testimony of one of the participants who appeared here as a protected witness, who spoke about his involvement in the conflict between the forces of the autonomous province of Western Bosnia and the forces of Izetbegovic's 5th Corps, saying that they worked as instructors in the capacity of either volunteers or mercenaries, and it was in no way related to any claim that they had been hired out from the police force of the Republic of Serbia, because if anybody was paying anybody, they were paid by the people who they worked for, and they worked for the autonomous province of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us hear the question now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police officers that -- the 400 to 500 police officers that you testified left from the RSK were issued Republic of Serbia MUP uniforms to work putting down a demonstration against Mr. Milosevic, was that a short-term assignment or was it in the nature of a long-term assignment or hiring of them by the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a short-term assignment. I think it only lasted three or four days, five days maximum, because they were already back by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they returned, did they return to their original positions within the RSK police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic also asked you about medical care. Other than the medical care that you described in your testimony, which you have testified was actually a way of expelling elderly Croats, were you ever aware of any legitimate attempt by the 21st Corps to render medical assistance to Croats living within the 21st Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always denied, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was denied?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if -- so are you testifying that there were cases where Croats requested medical assistance and it was actually denied?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there were requests coming through the ECMM for medical assistance to certain Croatian elderly persons in those villages, and those requests were denied on the basis that we don't even have for ourselves, let alone for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the parade on St. Vitus Day. What was the purpose of the massive show of military force that we saw in the videotape, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously the purpose was purely for the PR reasons, I mean to show the Croats how well we are armed, and also to show to the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has put to you that it would not be unusual for members of other units, particularly Republic of Serbia MUP units and units from the VRS or the Yugoslav People's Army, to participate in a celebration like this one. Were you able to determine which units there were guests at this celebration and which were part of the display of military force?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a reasonable way of actually assessing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us how it was you were able to distinguish between guests and actual members of this military display?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By their positions on the dais. That would be one thing. The other thing would be the introduction to President Martic at the time, the way it was carried out. Also the vehicles used in the procession, in the parade, those that belonged to the 21st Corps, or any other corps of the RSK army, did have their own number plates, and I have shown the Cyrillic letter "Z" on the number plates which belonged to the 21st Corps. Those vehicles which carried rocket systems that were brought from Republika Srpska had their number plates removed, and then after the parade they were put back on and taken out of RSK into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be reasonable for us to conclude that if these rocket launchers were simply guests of the celebration, that it would have been unnecessary to have removed the VRS number plates?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If they are guests, why hide?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the excerpt of the video that was displayed here in Court, there were a number of men in dress blue uniforms in front of the podium. Do you recall those men?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify from where they came?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the parade uniform of those members indicates they belonged to a special brigade in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was their function, or were you able to tell what their function was by their position at the podium?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An honourary one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has suggested that you were not known in KOS and that you were nothing more than a simple interpreter. During your time in the Krajina, were there other people in Knin that were as qualified as yourself to interpret between Serbian and English?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Knin, sir. I assume there were people who were very qualified in all of the RSK or Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of these people who would be equally qualified, would it be fair to say that a large number of them were actually from Knin or actually from the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that -- this group of people I'm now referring to, these people who were able to interpret as well as you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- were they actually born in the area or were they, like yourself, from outside the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Most of them were from the outside. I remember a lady that -- actually, she's an American, married to a guy from Krajina. She ended up in there during the war, and she translated for General Musa Bamayi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there a number of these interpreters, however, that were in fact from the area, born there, and living there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably 75 to 80 per cent of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason that you can think of why it was necessary for you to accompany the RSK delegation as an interpreter and to pretend to be from Knin, as opposed to one of these other people from the area actually serving as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there is a reason for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that reason?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that I have been given a specific task by Colonel Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has suggested to you that the members of the ARSK army who were officers were simply members of the Yugoslav army who were born in the RSK and simply remained there. Now, my question to you is: Of these officers who may have been born in the RSK, how many of them maintained their homes outside of the RSK and in the Belgrade area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where would their families have lived?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were in Serbia. Wherever they had their apartments or houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So other than the fact that they were born in the Krajina, did they have any current connection to the Krajina regarding family or place of residence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some of the officers would have a visit by their wives every now and then coming from Belgrade and going back, but none of them lived permanently in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has put it to you that it in fact was the Supreme Defence Council of the RSK that was the legal and factual organ in charge of the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. My question to you is: During your time in the 21st Corp headquarters, did you ever see any orders from the SDC of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe only one, and it was signed by Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the substance of that order was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to open the fight all along the DMZ in the case of any attack or a provocation by the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you spent in the headquarters of the 21st Corps, did you ever hear Colonel Bulat call or confer with any member of the SDC of RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, under the law of the former Yugoslavia, during times of war, police units would be placed under the authority of the army. At any time during your many conversations with Toso Pajic, did he ever indicate to you that he was receiving instructions from the SDC of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the four peace negotiations that you attended, were there ever any members of the Republic of Srpska Krajina SDC present on those -- to represent or to negotiate military matters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, not even one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've described in great detail for us the conversations that the delegation had with people in Belgrade. To your knowledge, were there ever any discussions or phone calls made to a member of the SDC of the RSK during the peace conferences that you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my presence, not even one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic has put it to you that your statement was in fact based upon your reading of the indictment and incorporating the assertions made in the indictment into your statement. The indictment was written and issued in November of 2001. What year did you give your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, from February to June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two years before the indictment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has also asserted that your testimony here is, at least in part, due to some type of benefits that you're receiving from your cooperation. I would ask you to briefly compare the quality of life you have now as compared to what you had in Belgrade before you decided to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have to say that during my life in Belgrade, I had a much, much better standard of living than I do now. It's only fair to remind you, because we talked about it, I left a Porsche and Mercedes at home, and God knows what, not in the house. I walked out of the country, sir, with a very, very small briefcase when I left Yugoslavia. I left everything behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider your relocation and your new identity a benefit that you have received or a measure to ensure your security?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be for the reason of ensuring my security, sir, not as an award for me testifying.
