utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has characterised your testimony as a betrayal of your colleagues and of Serbia. Back in 1991, 1992, can you describe for us whether or not you believed in the Serb cause at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I believed it with all my heart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at that time consider yourself to be a loyal Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider myself even today to be a loyal Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My final question to you, sir, is: Mr. Milosevic, yesterday, said the following, at page 88 of the transcript: "There were all kinds of excesses there. There probably were. Whenever hundreds, thousands of people are involved, injustice and excess is a common occurrence." Based on your actual observations of the excesses and injustices that you witnessed, how many of them were inevitable and how many of them were avoidable?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about actually the refugees being taken from Yugoslavia back into Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about all the injustices that you've described in your two days of testimony here, both perpetrated against Serbs, against Croats --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There were quite a few which were unavoidable and totally unnecessary, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic went on to say: But that these excesses and injustices were not an official policy. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I would rather believe that they are the part of the official policy of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of whose policy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, that concludes your evidence to the International Tribunal. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do go -- it doesn't concern you. Go, by all means. But I've just got to give an order in relation to the accused. I'm requested to make a formal order that he be given the opportunity to meet his associates this evening at the Tribunal. I make that order. We'll adjourn now until half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called, if I might take a moment just to take stock, as it were, regarding what exhibits the Prosecution has introduced with the last witness. The Prosecution has introduced Exhibit 336.SL, and that was a marked photocopy of the map, page 20. 347.5, the Prosecution at this stage would request that that still remain marked for identification and we are not tendering it at this time. And the Prosecution Exhibits 347.1.SL, .3.SL, .4.SL, and .5.SL, they were photographs, the Prosecution was tendering them. Regarding Prosecution Exhibit 348, all tabs from 1 through 19, with tab 17 being under seal, and the Prosecution will produce a redacted version of that tomorrow morning. And finally, Prosecution Exhibit 349, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is C-034, but in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. The next witness is C-034, but C-034 decided a couple of days ago and communicated with the Victims and Witnesses Unit to this effect; that he would prefer to give evidence without any protection at all. And so I call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is only going to produce three exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Mustafa Candic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, were you born in March of 1956 in or near Brcko, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? In due course, and we can have all of your background if it's material, did you become a Captain First Class in the Central Counter-Intelligence Group of the security organs of the air force and air defence forces in Zemun, in Serbia, taking that office in 1988?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was born on the 24th of March, 1956, not the 19th of February, 1956. And yes, it is true that I took up my service in the Central Counter-Intelligence Group of the security organs of the air force and air defence and I took up that position in December 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the date of February was translated to you. If it can give you any more confidence, I think I said March 1956 and something went wrong somewhere. Very well. Overall, after 15 years in the JNA, you left the service of that army on the 19th of February, 1992, and the reason for your leaving was what? Just tell us straight away.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that I left the former Yugoslav People's Army on the 19th of February, 1992. There are countless reasons for which I decided to take that important step, because I was conscious of the fact that by taking that step I was putting into question my whole existence and the livelihood of my family as well. However, of these countless reasons, I'm going to mention just one. Through my operational work and my work in the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, I arrived by certain information through my operational work, and I saw with my very own eyes, and I moved around the territory, both of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and, as I say, I saw that the Yugoslav People's Army, as an institution, throughout the whole of the former Yugoslavia, was, to all intents and purposes, de jure and de facto, had taken the side of just one ethnic group, namely, that group being the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Candic. You are ethnically a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Correct. I am --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all you --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I am a Muslim ethnically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all you need say. And I want you to turn to the force for which you worked, the Counter-Intelligence Group, which can be called KOG, I think, and we're going to look at a chart soon to show how the various intelligence and counter-intelligence units were formed. But just dealing with KOG itself, did KOG focus on three topics: Foreign intelligence services, Yugoslav emigre communities, and what's called the internal enemy?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when talking about the Counter-Intelligence Group, within its composition it had three separate entities, three separate wholes. One of those was the sector, or department, or entity, which focused on foreign intelligence services, and it investigated them and researched them. The second element, the second entity, looked into hostile emigre groupings, Yugoslav emigres. And the third entity dealt with the internal enemy, that is to say all those elements and components whose object it was to overthrow the system, to undermine the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I ask you a question that's susceptible to an answer yes, if you feel you can just deal with it in that way, it will save us some time. So my proposition was correct, and I think - just yes or no - you were engaged in the internal enemy section. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With an area of responsibility that included Kosovo and 19 municipalities in the north-east of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but you were also empowered to or instructed to conduct investigations elsewhere in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: That also is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Promoted to major in 1990, you became one of the four assistant chiefs of the central KOG, K-O-G, and Colonel Tomislav Cuk was the head of the central KOG?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: It is true that on the 22nd of December I was promoted to the rank of major in the aviation, before my time, and I became one of the four assistant chiefs in the centre of KOG in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Cuk was subordinated to Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tomislav Cuk was the head of the Counter-Intelligence Group, and yes, he was subordinated to Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic, who was the head of the security department in the command of air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber may have binders of exhibits, and the first one that I'm going to turn to is the chart. If the binder could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And therefore, I think the chart will be tab 1 of that exhibit. May the English version of this go on the overhead projector. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the position, Mr. Candic, this: That you prepared, in handwriting, which is available for the accused to consider if he wishes to, and others, you prepared a handwritten chart setting up the organisational structure, which has been converted by others into an English-language version of the same, and you are happy to explain what is necessary to explain from the English-language version, drawing to our attention straight away that because of the translation from your handwriting to typed script, there's one spelling mistake, namely, on the left-hand side, the name that reads at the moment Slobodan Kovacevic should in fact read Slobodan Rakocevic, R-A-K-O-C-E-V-I-C?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I did write this in my own hand. I drew up the chart, showing the system of the security in the armed forces of the former JNA. This schematic presentation, the chart that I see here, in the English version does not correspond to the chart I myself drew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's drawn from it. And if you would be good enough to help us, please, with the parts of the English chart that are material to the Judges. Is it right that there's a security administration at the centre, a federal secretariat for National Defence, SSNO, and in brackets we have the name Aleksandar Vasiljevic beside it, he being an officer of general rank and in charge? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The security administration as the top level in the system of security within the armed forces did exist, and at the head of that security administration was General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now look below that box and to the right, where you can see references to the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given a copy of that chart, please? In this set that I have received, I can't see the chart. I just see the rules of service, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should be behind "1." Look in tab 1. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is below and to the right of the block headed "SSNO" relates to the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th army and some other units with which we are not concerned today, Mr. Candic. To the left is the area that you can help us with, and that relates to the air force and AA defence security department for whom the security head was Slobodan Rakocevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We then see, branching off and to the right of that, three KOS counter-intelligence service headquarters sections identified. Were you working in one of those?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should it not be KOG instead of KOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It should be KOG.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It should be KOG.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were working in one of those?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The official title or name was never KOS. The official title in the armed forces of the former Yugoslav People's Army, or the former Yugoslavia, if you like, was the security service in the armed forces, and within the frameworks of the security service, there were the organs of security within units, that is to say, uniformed officers, and there were counter-intelligence groups as well, once again officers working in civilian clothes, plain clothes, officers who had quite different assignments compared to the officers who were in the units, which is where there were soldiers, officers, and the whole technical staff as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just deal with His Honour Judge Kwon's particular query. We see on this chart, which is probably a reflection of what you wrote, or may have been, KOS. Should that read KOS or KOG, or neither?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: On this chart, where it says KOS, it should be KOG, Counter-Intelligence Group, KOG, on the left-hand side, if that's what you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we move from there, we've been hearing about something called K-O-S, KOS, throughout this part of the case. Perhaps we could have that described.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help the Judges, please, with whether the term "KOS" was used, however improperly, and to what KOS related when it was used.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Of course I can explain that. The term KOS, K-O-S, was exclusively used among the people, and this term was left over from the Second World War, the counter-intelligence service. However, this World War II KOS term was transformed later on to become, within the Yugoslav People's Army, the security service of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the official title was the security service, and not KOS, K-O-S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be KOG and KOS is a hangover. Staying with this chart, we can see on the left-hand side linked to the air force and AA Defence Command Security Unit, security sections 1, 3, and 5, and the mark underneath it, "(uniform - worked within units in the immediate area). A sentence of explanation about what these were, because these were not, I think, where you were working, but just a sentence of explanation about that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I did not work there while I was working in the KOG, but before that, yes, I did, in one of those sections. And they are subordinate units to the command of the air force and air defence, and they were security sections. First of all, the 1st Air Corps, the 3rd Air Corps, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the 5th Air Corps. The 1st had its headquarters, its seat in Belgrade, the 3rd had its seat in Nis, and the 5th Air Corps had its headquarters in Zagreb. And of course, in those corps you had security sections, just as you did in the command security unit for air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see from the general picture presented by this chart that, of course, as well as the air force there were the armies and indeed somewhere there's, I think, a navy element to be considered as well maybe, I'm not sure. But can you just help us with this: Did the air force and its security have some particular interest or particular scope of responsibility greater than that enjoyed by the army units of like type?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The air force department of the command security unit and all the units on the left-hand side of the chart were spread out throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So, for example, the security section for war defence and anti-aircraft defence was more important than the security sections in the army or the navy, because their areas of responsibility were far smaller than the security department for the air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The air force really had authority over the whole territory as opposed to local authority or more restricted authority for the armies, correct, the individual armies?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Chains of command next. We'll look at what should happen in due course, but -- or should happen according to the law, but in one of these KOGs, one of these KOGs of which you were a member, the lines of command would appear to go first to the air force and air defence command security unit and then back to the security administration under Aleksandar Vasiljevic. How did the chain of command work in practice when you were engaged in exercises of a security kind?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: When I worked in the realm of security, the chain of command, or the professional leadership of the security organs down the vertical line or hierarchy, would go as follows: From the lower security organs up to the next step up the ladder, and then one rung more up the ladder, until the security administration was reached, and the head of that security administration, who was Aleksandar Vasiljevic. You were not allowed to skip a step. You had to go step by step, in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the theory of it. And did that mean that you would find intelligence decisions, in theory, being reported to individual units that weren't exclusively security units? For example, one of the KOG units, should it be reporting to the air force and air defence unit itself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: We were not allowed, nor did we do something like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it went straight up to Vasiljevic through the various rungs in the ladder?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we now look at the same exhibit, 350, the passage that the -- or the entry in that exhibit that the accused referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see, please -- is it tab 2? Tab 2, and it's paragraphs 16 and 17. It can be laid on the overhead projector, please, in English, and we'll provide a B/C/S version of the same paragraphs for the witness. And it may be appropriate, if we can find it, just to lay the title of the book in the B/C/S on the overhead projector for those viewing so they can see that it's an extract from the rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, as it's described. Just lay the title on the overhead projector briefly as well, so we can see what we're looking at. Thank you. And then we'll take that away and look at paragraphs 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs 16 and 17 read as follows: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the command officer of the command unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work, while JNA security organs, in organisations for NVO, are responsible to the competent assistant federal secretary for National Defence." And then paragraph 17: "The federal secretary for National Defence or a military officer authorised by him manages JNA security organs with regard to the application of the methods and means for the work of those organs." Did the way the chain of command in fact worked match with these requirements of your rules of service, Mr. Candic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: No. This is -- it did not really correspond to what is written here in this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that because, as you've already explained, the chain of command was via security groupings and personnel straight up to Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. So there was a vertical line, the professional line that went all the way up to General Vasiljevic. And what it says here, that the security organs are subordinate and responsible to the next superior officer is just something that was written on the paper. They were assistant commanders. But if I were to express it in percentages, I would say that that represented some 10 per cent, and the 90 per cent was done in accordance with this vertical line and reporting that went up to the next superior level, all the way up to the security administration and General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the result, did security officers at various levels have an authority that would be perhaps wider or narrower than their rank might suggest?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, their authorities, the authority of security officers, were always wider than their rank would indicate, in reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in a counter-intelligence unit. You were concerned with the internal enemy. And we are at the -- I think the beginning of the 1990s. Give, if you will, for those who may not have acquaintance with countries with this kind of security penetration, give a picture of how -- to what degree organisations and businesses, schools, would be penetrated by the intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it was illegal -- and when I say "illegal," that means that what security organs did at the time was not in accordance with the legislation. However, despite that, in 1989, in 1990, in 1991, pursuant to instructions and orders of the head of security administration, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and head of the security section of my own security section, Colonel Rakocevic, we created a network of collaborators who were our sources of information, and we did that in all spheres of civilian society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "all spheres," I raise a couple of hypothetical examples. If you had a small business of 50 employees, would you expect such a business to be penetrated? If you had a small local school with perhaps ten teachers, would you expect there to be penetration to a school of that size?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The main goal of penetrating all spheres of society, and that includes schools, companies, and so on, so the main goal was to infiltrate the authorities and police of the relevant republic. Naturally, I need to add that the media, this sphere of economy, of education, were something that were considered to be a target of interest of the security organs, because they wanted to find collaborators in those spheres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was going to turn to the bodies you've just described in a minute, but just to conclude my question, were businesses targeted as well? Were schools targeted, or not? So that we can have a picture of life in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I will repeat once again: All segments of society were targeted, including schools and companies, and the main goal, or the main interest, were the organs of authority and police organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... irrespective of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By law, were your -- was your service allowed to investigate civilians in the ordinary course of events?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: By law, the security organs of armed forces were never permitted to conduct investigations against civilians or for civilians unless those civilians acted against armed forces. But even in those cases, security organs had an obligation to submit a written request to relevant ministries of internal affairs, and had an obligation to conduct such operations in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior and state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In practice, by the time we're speaking of, was your service investigating civilians without going through those formalities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: In practice - and now I'm referring to 1989, 1990, 1991 - the security service placed the focus of its work precisely on civilians and did not report the Ministries of the Interior about that, nor did it inform competent authorities or organs of the state security service. Moreover, it looked for collaborators in the state security organs themselves, from which they were supposed to get a permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you could judge, was reporting on this non-legal form of investigation effected up to Vasiljevic's level? So far as you could judge, was he authorising or not this type of unlawful investigation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and Slobodan Rakocevic were the initiators of this process that I described. This was done pursuant to their order. No security organ would dare do something like this without informing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move on, something not in the summary but that is in the statement. The accused, the amici can find it at page 4. Was there an occasion, either 1990 or 1991, in the course of which Rakocevic made reference to the accused and also to the Academy of Science?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a situation, or rather, a special meeting with the members of the Central Counter-Intelligence Group which worked in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, because, as you could see from that first diagram, the Central Counter-Intelligence Group had three detachments. The first one was in Skopje, the second in Zagreb, and the third one in Sarajevo. So from the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, collaborators sent in reports to the security organs of the Counter-Intelligence Group, based on which additional reports were made which were then directly sent to Rakocevic and General Vasiljevic, who was the head of the security administration. At that meeting that I mentioned, the meeting called by Slobodan Rakocevic, he was visibly angry because he did not have an opportunity to read basically a single report from Belgrade. And he explained this anger of his by saying that the Serb Academy of Science -- of Arts and Sciences was active in Belgrade, that they were working on a project called Memorandum, that the main initiator and author -- ideological initiator of this project was Slobodan Milosevic and that we, as security organs, had no information about what was going on in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is an officer of the rank of Slobodan Rakocevic, who was, I think -- what was he? A colonel at this stage? And the hard problem he was facing, or that you were facing, was that you were getting no intelligence from this particular quarter, whereas you were getting intelligence from your network of sources from basically everywhere else that you wanted to get intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: That's precisely so. So Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic in fact wanted to say that security organs of the Counter-Intelligence Group had no collaborators in Belgrade, which is where all the main decisions were made, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before I move on, was it surprising or was it standard and unsurprising for an officer at that rank and at that time to be linking problems in the way that we've just heard with the Academy of Science in the way that he did?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The way he did it was done, as far as I was able to understand it, because he saw in that memorandum, and also in the steps taken by Slobodan Milosevic, that that was a way to break up Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and disintegrate it, and at the same time create the Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 11 of the summary. In October 1991, a little later, after the 5th Air Force Corps retreated from Zagreb Bihac -- which the Chamber can find in its atlas, page 26, B-2. We don't need to place this on the overhead projector, this is, I think, really for the Chamber's reference. At the moment, in any event. Did you find yourself escorting people to investigate the radio transmitter at Bihac air base and did you stay there for some four days?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is right that sometime in late September or early Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. October - I can't remember the exact date - I received an order for Colonel Rakocevic to escort a column of three radio reconnaissance vehicles whose object was to detect, or rather, to use the method of radio trigonometry in order to find locations of radio amateur stations in the vicinity of the airport in Bihac, which supplied or sent reports to Zagreb via those ham radios and reported on every sortie or every take-off of airplanes from the Bihac airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, is it right that when there, you found that the security organs and the Counter-Intelligence Group of the 5th Air Force Corps had been relocated to the hunting lodge at Bihac, and you then met a friend of yours, Major Cedo Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I first handed over these vehicles to Colonel Topalovic who was head of security section of the 5th Air Force Corps at the Bihac airport. At the time, he was drunk. When I came, when I arrived, I was able to see several fires in the vicinity of the Bihac airport, in the evening hours. He was angry. I asked him what it was about. He told me that all airplanes had taken off from the Bihac airport and almost burned down the village called Vaganac, or Zegar or something like that, I don't remember. And I was able to see that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is not in the summary, Your Honour, but on page 5 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move forward if we can, please, Mr. Candic. If I'm right in what I've described to you as background events leading up to your re-encountering Major Knezevic, can we move on to this: Did you then also see at the hunting lodge some members of the SDB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: When I came to Bihac, I didn't know exactly what Cedo Knezevic was, so I asked Colonel Topalovic about that, and he told me where he was and gave me a vehicle which took me to the hunting lodge where Major Knezevic was. In the hunting lodge, in addition to Colonel Knezevic, there were several other members of the 2nd Detachment of the Counter-Intelligence Group of the air force and air defence, but there were also several uniformed individuals who did not have official insignia of the JNA, and also several members of the regular military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discover whether there were members of the SDB of Serbia there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: There were members of the SDB of Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discover how it was they came to be there? If so, how did you make that discovery? Was it from what they told you or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I knew that some members of the SDB of Serbia, primarily those that had fled from the Republic of Croatia, namely, Serbs that used to work for the Croatian SDB, that they transferred to the SDB of Serbia, and occasionally they would go to Bihac, Lika, Banija, Kordun, where they would head paramilitary formations in those areas. Naturally, prior to going to these areas that I just mentioned, they would all go to the hunting lodge in Bihac, where Major Knezevic was also present, and some other operatives of the 2nd Detachment of the Counter-Intelligence Group of air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whatever their history at the time of their deployment or redeployment to Bihac, and as you understood it, they were formally members of the Serbian SDB?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on now to what you learnt from Major Knezevic. Did you discover that he was conducting operations there with, amongst others, Lieutenant Colonel Dusan Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I discovered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you that he indeed had been assigned a special task?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: He didn't say that to me on his own. I simply asked him whether he was just lying and sleeping there or actually doing something, because I did not receive any reports of his in Belgrade. And then he started explaining his mission to me, his assignment. Specifically, he told me that he had a direct link with the security administration and General Vasiljevic, that he was in charge of the operational -- operation called Proboj 1, or Breakthrough 1, that certain Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic from the 5th military district was heading that operation and that he was his deputy. When I asked him what was the object, the purpose of that operation, he told me that its object was to arm the Serbs in Banija, Lika, Kordun, and Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there for one second. Those areas can be - and they're areas rather than towns - can be found on the atlas, page 20, at letter C-3 and thereabouts. And you'll be looking -- in fact, if I hold up my atlas, you'll be looking at the words that come with the single letters spread out across the page, because they're describing the areas, and you can see two of them where I'm indicating, running up the map, roughly in the middle. Kordun and Banija. They're a little hard to see. Now, he told you that was the object of the exercise, and I'm going to ask you in due course what parts of this you saw evidenced yourself and whether in other parts you were just dependent on what Knezevic told you. But did he explain to you how this arming process was to take place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, he did. He did explain how this entire process was supposed to develop. He told me that through collaborators, people who used to collaborate with us, and the leaders of the SDS from the areas I mentioned, that those people would personally come to him, and to Lieutenant Colonel Smiljanic, and give them their requests in terms of weaponry, ammunition, and so on, so that they could prepare and carry out certain operations in those areas and put up resistance to Croats, because at the time there was a war going on in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what he explained to you. Did you see any of this happening yourself or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The first thing I asked him was, "Where did you get the weapons from? How can you distribute them?" And he said he was distributing them from the depot of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the next evening he would show me some of these depots, and that is exactly what he did. I had the opportunity to visit three such depots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what quantity of weapons did you find in them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, in those three depots that I visited - I didn't see them all and I didn't even know the total number of depots - the three depots I did see were half empty, but in all of the three taken together, there was enough weapons to arm 20.000 to 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were records kept of this arming process and of the issue of arms to individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: It is purely by chance that I learned that very precise records are kept about weapons issued to individuals, indicating exact amounts. I learned that one evening when I was lying on a bed in a room which served as an office-come-rest room, while Major Knezevic was typing out reports. At one point I asked him if I could give him a hand. I got up and approached him from behind, and he said he didn't need any assistance. But I could see over his shoulder the sheet in the typewriter, and I could see the heading: "Operation Proboj 1." I could see the date and contents, as indicated, namely, activities related to the arming of Serbs for such-and-such a day. Below the contents, I also saw the names of people to which these weapons were distributed. I couldn't stand behind his back a long time, because I didn't want to bother him, but still I could see that all the names were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see to whom this letter was addressed, or were you told to whom this letter was addressed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Right there on the right-hand side, it said, "Security Administration, to General Vasiljevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness now look at and may we view on the overhead projector the last exhibit of the three to be produced, Exhibit 350, I think it's tab 3. If the usher would be good enough to place the first page of the Cyrillic version on the overhead projector, to begin with, then place the last page of the Cyrillic version with the signature line on it on the overhead projector. We can see that this is a letter dated the 16th of October, or 15th of October -- I think 16th, actually, of 1994, and that it comes from Dusan Smiljanic, the man to whom you've referred and with whom Knezevic was working at the time. If the usher could be good enough now to place, please, page 3 of the English version - that's page 3 at the bottom - on the overhead projector, and if Mr. Candic could please have the registry page 02009470 before him, which is the third sheet of the original version. Thank you very much. Your Honours, this is a long letter, and it's a letter that goes to General Mladic, as we saw briefly, from Smiljanic, and of course, it's a historic letter with a number of complaints and concerns he raises. And although they may be of interest, they're not necessarily material to our inquiries here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the page we're looking at, do we see the following text in this letter, please, Mr. Candic, and at the first passage you're looking at, is there this: "At the beginning of August 1991, on a task given by the UB/ Security Administration, the Proboj-2 operational team was formed under my leadership..." and then some further references to that. And then if we go down the page to the next paragraph, do we find the following: "In the period from August to October 1991 we distributed or withdrew from what are now Ustasha depots about 20.000 assorted weapons, and our involvement in military organising and the performance of professional security tasks to a high standard, among other things, was well known to General Kelecevic too. This can also be documented from reports." If we go further down the page, to save time, and towards the bottom, picking it up at "In Bihac": "In Bihac, in January 1991, I accepted the duty of chief of security in the 10th Corps..." He then sets out his superiors and some references to other officers. And then right down, further down: "A considerable number of officers, especially those from the area, were utterly demoralised..." And then further on, right at the foot of the page: "By agreement with the OB, I organised OB and individual officers from the police for the organised arming of Serbs in the town itself. I do not remember, but I think that about 5.000 assorted infantry weapons were distributed. The logistics base, headed by Colonel Skondric, was the supply source for the arming." And then over the page: "As the forming of the unit had begun, we were asked to engage officers who came from those areas in it immediately." And then he goes on. And perhaps that's all I need cover on that. Now, I'll come back to the reference to Proboj 2 in a second, but so far as the passage in the letter dealing with the arming of Serbs, does that accord with what you've told us and what you experienced, Mr. Candic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: What I saw and what you read, and I read too, tallies 100 per cent, although I really didn't know about this document. The code is right, and my assessment of the weapons already distributed seems to be right, as well as the locality where all that happened. I am simply speechless. I believe all this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the letter, the exercise of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise this very briefly: It's been referred to by my learned friend as a historical letter, however, it's very unclear as to what this witness can actually say about the letter, although he can say something about its content. The Trial Chamber has been relatively strict in relation to letters put forward by the accused, and perhaps Your Honours would consider the admissibility of this document, given that the witness has stated that he can say nothing really about the fact of the letter itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Higgins, the letters which the accused has put forward have been letters which were supplied to him, for him to cross-examine. We've allowed him to cross-examine upon them. We haven't allowed him to put them in as exhibits, for the very good reason that there mainly ammunition for cross-examination and he can call evidence about it. This document, and the Prosecution can deal with its authenticity, is one which I should have thought speaks for itself, and we really, I would have thought, required no further evidence about it, but we will ask the Prosecution if they can add anything by way of confirming it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, its provenance can be dealt with shortly. It is a document that speaks for itself. I use the word "historic" Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because of course it's dated 1994 and it's therefore reflections by the author of earlier events. That doesn't change its essential admissibility. The ability of this witness to identify passages in it that accord with his own experience is helpful in relation both to the document itself when we seek to lay it before you and, in a sense, confirming his evidence, so it's a useful and proper exercise. And I'll come back, if I may, in a minute or so to the precise provenance of this document falling into our hands. May I move on and come back to that? Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letter, insofar as we're able to consider it, Mr. Candic, refers to the period August to October 1991, and also refers to something called Proboj 2. We heard from the interpreters what "Proboj" means in translation. Was there a Proboj 2 exercise of which you became aware?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: It is true that I also found about an operation called Proboj 2. It was an operation which again had the objective of arming Serbs, but this time in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, and the operation was led by Major Ljuban Karan from the Central Counter-Intelligence Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for just a second? No criticism of the way you're giving your evidence but just to make matters easier for the Chamber. From whom did you learn the -- learn of this project, and was it something you saw yourself at all or are you entirely dependent on what you were told about it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: As for the Operation Proboj 2, I'm relying on things I heard, but also on things I saw with my own eyes. Before learning anything directly, I heard certain things about it. Namely, shortly after I learned about the Operation Proboj 1 in Belgrade, or, more precisely, in Zemun, Major Cedo Knezevic arrived, and that day he -- Major Ljuban Karan and I had coffee together, on which occasion Major Ljuban Karan, who was in charge of Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, complained that Serbs in those parts lack weapons. Then Cedo Knezevic offered his good services and said, "Why didn't you say so before? I have enough weaponry to arm half of America." And he promised that as soon as he returned to Bihac, he would send two truckfuls of weapons to him. These two trucks indeed arrived. However, they arrived when Major Karan Ljuban was no longer there. He was away on mission in Eastern Slavonia with his team. And since the soldiers, the policemen who drove those two trucks didn't know what to do with the weaponry, I went to see Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic to ask what to do with these two trucks, believing that he was familiar with the whole project. Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic was rather angry and criticised me strongly. He dropped what he was doing, left his office, and ordered that these weapons be unloaded in one of the classrooms of a training centre for the Counter-Intelligence Group in Zemun. After that, this weaponry remained long after I left. As long as I was there, in fact, these weapons remained there. But the papers I later saw were headed "Operation Proboj 1" and then information was listed below that they had managed to gather. Later on, I heard things and learned things myself about an operation called Proboj 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the operation you've just been describing, involving Major Ljuban Karan, this is Proboj 2, and it was not successful because of the intervention of Rakocevic. What was the reason for his objection to the provision of these arms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I don't want to guess at the reasons. All I know is what he told me. He told me, "Why are you going over my head? We have the Yugoslav People's Army, and if there is a war to be waged, it will be waged by the JNA, not paramilitary formations." That's all I know. What the real reason was, or whether there was another reason, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this unsuccessful or almost totally unsuccessful Proboj 2, do the names Hadzic and Arkan become involved in some way?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Even before the Proboj 2 operation, which I learnt about and saw things about, I knew about both Goran Hadzic and Arkan. I knew they were close friends. While Goran Hadzic was a source of Major Ljuban Karan's named --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the code-name.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: They often travelled together, and there was no particular reason for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Hadzic's attitude towards the intelligence services of which you were a part change on his taking office of president?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, Hadzic's attitude was such that he never even made an appearance in the Central Counter-Intelligence Group. He was a collaborator, a source of Major Ljuban Karan's. However, Major Ljuban Karan, without being very open about it, often was wont to say that Hadzic had a very good relationship with members of the SDB of Serbia and people from the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, that he has a good reputation and enjoys great authority as the president of the autonomous province of Slavonia, Baranja, and Eastern Srem -- or rather Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, within the overall setting of the Proboj 2 dealings or preparations, did you learn from Ljuban Karan anything about Arkan's involvement in either volunteers or the provision of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, from Major Ljuban Karan, I also learnt things about Arkan. Major Ljuban Karan had only good things to say about him, and he said that were it not for Arkan and his volunteers, Serbs in Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem would come to a bad end, but thanks to him, the Serbs are holding out well in Krajina, and Arkan, in his words, was doing all that the Yugoslav People's Army was supposed to do, whereas the army itself is keeping a low profile, being inferior to him and his force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, in the event, were some -- to your knowledge, were some limited number of weapons from the Proboj 2 project eventually distributed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon return from Slavonia, when he learned that these two trucks were unloaded at the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, Major Karan went to see Rakocevic. He was very angry. He wanted the entire amount of weaponry to be issued to him, to transfer to Eastern Slavonia. However, he didn't get his way because Rakocevic told him that he would get a few barrels, meaning a few rifles, but exclusively for high-quality sources and collaborators, as reward for their work. And as far as I know, on that occasion Ljuban Karan managed to get only seven or eight barrels out of the entire consignment and drive them away by car. The rest, as I said, remained in that classroom at the Central Counter-Intelligence Group headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on from Proboj 2, the letter, Exhibit 350, tab 3, was produced to an investigator who will be a witness and who is in a position, I think, to give evidence from the author, acknowledging authenticity of the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Proboj 2, was there a plan for Proboj 3, but Proboj 3 was wholly unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the initiative of Major Ljuban Karan, to whom Lisica Darvin, from a subordinate security organ, married to a woman from Ljubuski, this other man was forced by Karan to create a network of sources in that area --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll cut you very short, because as it was unsuccessful, we need know no more than this: The intention was to arm what geographical area and what population?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, again, the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the area we've just been considering is on page 23, at D-2 in the atlas. I move to paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, or were there efforts pursued to distribute weapons in north-eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: It's not that efforts were made. Rather, the arming of Serbs in the north-eastern Bosnia, where I was an operative in charge of reporting on the situation in that area regarding arming of Serbs in that area, I, as security officer, classified them along three lines. The first line relates to first information I managed to collect on the arming of Serbs in northern Bosnia is that from the 17th Corps, a large amount of weapons were driven away to Mount Ozren, near Tuzla, and stored in abandoned mines. I want to remind you that Mount Ozren is populated exclusively by Serbs. There were no units of the JNA or even reserve positions. And I saw absolutely no reason why weapons from official depots would be driven to some mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours can find Ozren Mountain to the west of Tuzla, page 28, C-2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the absence of any JNA units, the inference to be drawn by you was what, that the weapons were to be handed over to whom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Leaders of the SDS. I was informed by my sources that these were people who worked in the state security service, who also had networks of collaborators of their own, collecting their own intelligence, and it was them who supplied me with reports of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second line -- you've referred to three lines, in your own terminology. The second line?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The second line of the arming of Serbs in north-eastern Bosnia, and I would even say in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, was through the proclaimed mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everybody was supposed to respond to the call-up: Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. However, shortly afterwards, the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, made an appeal to Bosniaks and Croats not to respond to the call-up, and those who had already responded, he said, should leave their units and go home. In that way, the civilian population that was mobilised from the reserve force consisted entirely of Serbs who had joined units of the army as reservists, were issued with weapons and equipment, and in that way they were armed, on the one hand; and on the other hand, they were very well paid for their work as reservists. I also know that they were allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third line, then, of the three you've characterised?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The third line was as follows, when we're talking about the arming of Serbs in north-eastern Bosnia. That is something that reminded me to a great extent to what was happening in Bihac, in the hunting lodge there, and something that I talked about when I spoke about Major Cedo Knezevic and Lieutenant Colonel Dusan Smiljanic. On one occasion, when I had gone to north-eastern Bosnia, Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Dzigurski, who was very close to individual members of the state security services of Serbia, the SDB, told me that he had agreed with Major Cedo Knezevic that Cedo Knezevic, from Bihac, should send a small transport vehicle of the pinzgauer type, the police type of pinzgauer vehicle, with weapons and ammunition, and this to be sent to a certain Stevo Todorovic, from the village of Slatina, close to Bosanski Samac. He asked me that the vehicle that was driven by the policeman belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army, to wait for it between Derventa and Doboj, to meet it there on that stretch of road. And that as I knew the terrain around north-eastern Bosnia, that I should go to the village of Slatina beforehand to find Stevo Todorovic, and to have these weapons unloaded there for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now deal with your reporting. When you sent reports to your superiors about these events - and by your superiors, I mean Rakocevic and Vasiljevic - were you allowed, encouraged, or otherwise, to make full reports of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, working in the Central Counter-Intelligence Group, objectively speaking, I did write about all the events that took place, and their details, in the area of my own responsibility, or rather, in the area of responsibility of north-eastern Bosnian, and among other things, I wrote about the activities of the leaders of the SDS, the leaders of the SDA, the HDZ parties, but also about the arming of all those three groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your reports accepted as drafted or were you encouraged in any way to modify them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: The reports that I wrote, when it came to the arming of Serbs and the activities of the SDS, this dominated, not because I was a Bosniak and then I tended to overemphasise this, to inflate it and to say that one side was more dangerous than the other and vice versa, but because I had received reports from my collaborators of this kind. And it was on the basis of how my superiors reacted to my reports, to what I would write, I was able to see that they did not attach any importance to some vital pieces of information which I sent up to them regarding the SDS and the arming of the Serbs in north-eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an occasion when you wanted to see General Vasiljevic about this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I did want to see General Vasiljevic, and I was very angry, because I received very reliable data, authentic information, about a decision taken by the leadership of the SDS to the effect that the non-Serbian population from Bijeljina and Zvornik, Bratunac, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica, should be dislocated to the Tuzla area, whereas the Serbian population from Tuzla and the environs of Tuzla should be relocated to the other regions: Bijeljina, Zvornik, Bratunac, and Srebrenica, which is to say along the banks of the River Drina. This report of mine was met, to put it mildly, with statements that this was impossible. However, I knew that it was a very serious report, because I knew who gave me the information, supplied me with information of this kind, and I was highly revolted and angry, and asked Colonel Cuk for a meeting with General Vasiljevic so that he could explain to me why the security service of the armed forces didn't think my report interesting enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to meet the general?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tomislav Cuk did not allow me to see the general. He just patted me on the back and said, "Muki, leave that alone for now. Don't go into that matter." And he did not permit me to have this meeting. But I could have gone on my own, sidestepped Colonel Cuk and gone to General Vasiljevic myself. However, I didn't do that, and I slowly began to put the pieces of the jigsaw puzzle together in my head, and that is why I subsequently left the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn to one or two other topics, a little bit more about General Vasiljevic. Though he was several rungs up the ladder from you, did you ever see him at your meetings? Did he attend your meetings? This is not in the summary. It's at page 4 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, as the chief of the security administration and one of the foremost authorities in the area, somebody who had a vast amount of knowledge and who was a great professional in his field, he was a guest in all the other departments, or rather, not a guest, but he tried to be present in all the departments, to visit all the departments, the navy and all the other security organs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... meeting of Colonel Rakocevic where General Vasiljevic was in attendance, where something was said about loyalty oaths that generals had been asked to sign up to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was present. I attended one of those meetings when General Aleksandar Vasiljevic -- and I never saw him more angry than he was then. He was prone to anger on occasion, but at that particular time he was beside himself with anger. And he told us that Slobodan Milosevic allowed himself the gall to ask the generals of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Serbs, to sign a loyalty oath to him. And his comment was so angry that he just told us that we should focus our activity towards the fact that not only the generals were coming under scrutiny, but that we should see whether there were others who opted in that way or declared themselves in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a date or approximate date for this meeting where Vasiljevic complained of being asked to sign a loyalty oath to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, that that was immediately before the events that came to pass in the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 20. And I have an eye on the clock. I don't know what time the Court is sitting until today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A quarter past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an incident involving a Catholic priest in which you became involved or in the end of which you became involved?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that incident involving a Catholic priest. I think, as far as I remember, that his name was Josip something or other. I'm not quite sure of his last name. Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic called me and issued an order to me that with Radojcic, a man named Radojcic, Radenko Radojcic, that I should report to him and to transfer that Catholic priest in a black Marija used by the police, a closed van, to the Brcko area, which was where Croats lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that, but did you at that time or thereabouts discover what had actually happened to the priest?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I accepted to carry out the orders of Colonel Slobodan Rakocevic and I reported to Radenko Radojcic. I came into contact with him and that was actually the first time that I learned about this Catholic priest. He told me that the man had been arrested somewhere in the Banija area and that they tried to convince him to cooperate and collaborate but that they had failed and that, for that reason, he was transferred to the Batajnica airport, into a room where he was locked up, and on that same day, when I went to take him over and transfer him to the Brcko area, I saw that he was in a very bad state, that he had been tortured, that he was exhausted, and that he was hardly able to stand up on his own two feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand or calculate the reason to be for his being taken thus to Brcko, or the Brcko area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA CANDIC
utterances.text: I would say that the reason for having him transferred to the Brcko area was, and particularly an area inhabited by Croats, was that the Croatian population should take him in as an elderly man and should help him. He wouldn't know where -- he wouldn't know where he had been. He couldn't have told them all the terrors that he had had to live through and experience, on the one side, and on the other hand, they would help him to go back to where he had come from, that is to say to Banija, or as Brcko is the frontier, the border with Croatia, to transfer him back to Croatia, and in that way, to instil fear and panic among the Croatian populace in the Posavina area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a convenient moment, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't be much longer tomorrow. I'm sorry it's been a little slower than I forecast, but I'll be finished in 20 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Candic, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning, 9.00. Could you be back then to continue your evidence, and could you remember in the adjournment not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Very well. 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of November 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
